Title: Trustworthy agentic AI systems: a cross-layer review of architectures, threat models, and governance strategies for real-world deployment [version 1; peer review: awaiting peer review]
Authors: Ibrahim Adabara; Bashir Olaniyi Sadiq; Aliyu Nuhu Shuaibu; Yale Ibrahim Danjuma; Venkateswarlu Maninti
Year & Venue: 2025; F1000Research, 14:905 (first published 11 Sep 2025; version 1, awaiting peer review); DOI 10.12688/f1000research.169927.1
Core Problem Addressed: Agentic AI systems with autonomous reasoning, memory augmentation, and adaptive planning introduce novel security risks, governance challenges, and ethical considerations that current frameworks (EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC) inadequately address; conventional layered security models designed for static computing architectures cannot defend adaptive, distributed agents (Sec. 1, p. 3).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: No system is proposed; the paper is a cross-layer narrative review that consolidates: (a) architectural paradigms (mono-agent, multi-agent, decentralized/federated, hybrid/blockchain-enabled) (Sec. 4, pp. 10-13); (b) a layered threat taxonomy (cognitive exploits, memory poisoning, prompt injection, shadow agents, federated governance risks, cross-layer propagation) (Sec. 5, pp. 13-19); (c) governance frameworks (OECD, EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ETHOS) (Sec. 6, pp. 20-27); and (d) defense architectures (SHIELD layered defense, Zero-Trust Architecture with runtime monitoring, SAGA cryptographic identity enforcement, ACD/AICA autonomous cyber defense) (Sec. 8, pp. 31-37). LLMs are framed as "cognitive cores" of agentic systems when augmented with external memory, planning modules, and orchestration layers (Sec. 3.1, pp. 7-8); human-in-the-loop safeguards are advocated for oversight, e.g., in military lethal decision-making and legal compliance (Sec. 7.2, p. 28; Sec. 9.6, p. 42).
Methodology: Narrative review (explicitly "a narrative synthesis rather than a systematic literature review"); sources: IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, ScienceDirect, arXiv, plus policy reports (OECD, NIST, European Commission) and NeurIPS/ICML/AAAI proceedings; keyword clusters ("agentic AI", "autonomous agents", "multi-agent systems", "cross-layer security", "trustworthy AI", "AI governance", "threat modeling") with Boolean operators; no strict temporal filter but priority to last five years; grey literature selectively included; conceptual-relevance inclusion criteria rather than rigid filtering; number of studies reviewed Not specified (full source list in supplementary Table A1) (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 2.1-2.2, pp. 4-5).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable as quantitative evidence: the paper reports no MTTD, MTTR, alert-fatigue, or resolution-time measurements. Qualitative mentions only: ReliaQuest's agentic AI for threat detection and incident response "has improved detection speed and reduced human workload" (Sec. 7.1, pp. 27-28); industries deploying Zero-Trust plus runtime monitoring "report significant reductions in breach impact and faster incident detection" (Sec. 8.2, p. 33); military agentic frameworks with 6G networks enhance capabilities "by reducing response times" (Sec. 7.2, p. 28). No baselines or percentages published.
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Comparative evaluation finds no architecture universally optimal: multi-agent systems gain scalability, emergent intelligence, and redundancy but increase attack surface, coordination complexity, and collusion vulnerability; hybrid/blockchain-enabled systems offer the best security/scalability/governance balance at high computational cost and latency (Sec. 4.5, Table 1, p. 13). Reported failure-mode figures: AI2 attack hijacking action-aware memory bypasses safety filters "with a success rate of over 99%" (Sec. 5.3, p. 15); InjecAgent benchmark shows "up to 24% success rates for indirect injections" against tool-integrated LLM agents (Sec. 5.3, p. 15); backdoor attacks on embodied LLM agents show "almost 100% success rates" (Sec. 5.2, p. 15); "even a 10% poisoning rate can severely degrade cooperation" in multi-agent swarms (Sec. 5.2, pp. 14-15). SAGA defense achieved secure enforcement "with negligible task utility degradation" across distributed agentic tasks (Sec. 8.3, p. 34).
Limitations / Future Work: Authors identify open gaps rather than a study-limitations section: incomplete alignment and meta-reasoning safeguards; hard-to-detect long-term memory corruption; high false negatives against indirect prompt attacks; weak insider governance; lack of holistic cross-layer anomaly correlation (Table 2, p. 19); lack of standardized cross-domain incident reporting; weak operationalization of governance; unpredictable emergent multi-agent behaviors; misaligned risk attitudes and liability voids; underdeveloped benchmarking needing observability-driven, multi-objective safety metrics (Sec. 9.9, Table 5, pp. 44-45). Future directions: adaptive/decentralized governance (e.g., ETHOS), memory-integrity architectures, federated agent revocation mechanisms, and interdisciplinary collaboration (Sec. 9, pp. 38-45; Sec. 10.3, p. 47). The narrative (non-systematic) methodology is acknowledged as deliberately flexible rather than reproducible (Sec. 2.1, p. 4).
Relevance to My Thesis: This review does not measure incident metrics, but it frames the trust, security, and governance preconditions for deploying an Agentic AI copilot in production incident response. The ReliaQuest case (autonomous agents for threat detection, incident response, and remediation workflows improving detection speed) is a directly relevant industrial precedent for MTTD/MTTR-oriented copilots, and the Zero-Trust plus runtime-monitoring discussion connects to automated observability pipelines. Its threat taxonomy (hallucination, goal drift, memory poisoning, prompt injection, shadow agents) enumerates failure modes a copilot could introduce into an incident-response loop, arguing for human-in-the-loop oversight. The identified gap in observability-driven benchmarking for non-deterministic agents supports my thesis motivation for empirically measuring MTTD/MTTR impacts of agentic copilots.
Relevance Score: Medium - directly centered on Agentic AI and multi-agent systems with cybersecurity incident-response deployment cases (ReliaQuest, ZTA), but purely a trustworthiness/governance review with no MTTD/MTTR measurement or AIOps evaluation.

Title: The role of agentic AI in shaping a smart future: A systematic review
Authors: Soodeh Hosseini; Hossein Seilani
Year & Venue: 2025; Array (Elsevier journal), vol. 26, article 100399
Core Problem Addressed: The rapid evolution of Agentic AI, including Generative AI (GenAI) agents, "has outpaced a cohesive understanding of its applications, challenges, and strategic implications"; the authors identify a gap in synthesizing Agentic AI's diverse capabilities (multimodal processing, hierarchical architectures, ML outsourcing) and in providing actionable adoption strategies for organizations. Not focused on IT operations, SRE, or incident response specifically (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 1, p. 1).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Narrative synthesis of Agentic AI concepts: key attributes (autonomy, goal-oriented behavior, environmental interaction, learning, workflow optimization, multi-agent systems) (Sec. 1.2, Table 1, pp. 2-3); hierarchical agent architecture with master agent, orchestrator agent, and micro-agents (e.g., FAQ, issue-resolution, status-update, feedback agents) (Sec. 4, Table 4, pp. 6-7); transition from assisted "Copilot" (human-in-the-loop assistant) to autonomous "Autopilot" models (Sec. 5, pp. 6-8); AI-as-a-Service/outsourcing model paying per resolved issue (e.g., Sierra support bots) (Sec. 4 and Sec. 6, pp. 6, 9); tool landscape covering LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, AutoGPT, LangChain, IBM Watson, Amazon SageMaker, TensorFlow, Llama (Sec. 7, pp. 10-12); and a GenAI strategy-formulation framework (vision/objectives, use-case prioritization, two-stage PoC-to-scale deployment, security, monitoring) (Sec. 8, pp. 12-13).
Methodology: ⚠ Ambiguous: the title says "systematic review" but the abstract states "This narrative review explores the role of Agentic AI" (Abstract, p. 1); no Kitchenham/PRISMA-style protocol, search strategy, inclusion/exclusion criteria, database list, or paper counts are reported anywhere in the article; it is a literature-based narrative/conceptual review citing 48 references, with no dataset, environment, or sample size (Abstract, p. 1; Secs. 1-9, pp. 1-14).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable — MTTD, MTTR, alert fatigue, and incident resolution time are never measured or mentioned; only adjacent secondary figures are cited from other sources: AI chatbots "decreased response times by 60 % while increasing customer satisfaction scores by 25 %" (Sec. 3, p. 4); predictive maintenance reduced equipment downtime by 20-50 % (Sec. 3, p. 4); AI outsourcing reducing diagnostic times by up to 30 % and enhancing equipment uptime by 20 % (Sec. 6.1, p. 9).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Reported (secondary, cited) impacts: AI-driven automation can improve productivity by up to 40 % (McKinsey, via [20]) (Sec. 3, p. 4); AIaaS with agentic hierarchies reduces operating costs by up to 30 % and increases response efficiency by 40-50 % (Sec. 4, p. 7); AIaaS adopters report 20-35 % operational-cost reduction within two years and ROI of 3x-5x over five years, with initial implementation costs of $50,000-$500,000 (Sec. 4.1, p. 5); hierarchical master/orchestrator/micro-agent structures are argued to increase overall system efficiency and coordination (Sec. 4, pp. 6-7; Sec. 9.1, p. 14); Copilot-to-Autopilot transition increases autonomy and efficiency but risks errors in complex scenarios, requiring human-in-the-loop safety nets (e.g., Sierra escalation to humans) (Secs. 5.2-5.3, pp. 7-8).
Limitations / Future Work: Authors state: "The limitations of this research include the limited review of existing tools and the lack of case analysis in specific industries" (Sec. 9.2, p. 14); future work: industry-specific, case-by-case studies; deeper study of ethical/social aspects (privacy, data security, labor-market impact); integration of Agentic AI with emerging technologies such as quantum computing and edge AI (Sec. 9.2, p. 14; Sec. 9, p. 13; Abstract, p. 1); other named directions: Explainable Agentic AI, People-to-AI collaboration, Federated Agentic AI (Sec. 5.4, p. 8).
Relevance to My Thesis: This review supplies the conceptual vocabulary my thesis builds on: it formalizes the "Copilot" (human-in-the-loop assistant) versus "Autopilot" (fully autonomous) spectrum, which directly frames the thesis positioning of Agentic AI as a Copilot during incident response. Its hierarchical master/orchestrator/micro-agent architecture and the issue-resolution/status-update agent roles map naturally onto incident-management pipelines, and its catalog of orchestration tools (LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, AutoGPT) informs prototype tool selection. The cited efficiency figures (60 % response-time reduction, 20-50 % downtime reduction) are only loose proxies, as the paper never addresses MTTD/MTTR, observability, or AIOps. It is therefore useful for background/related-work framing rather than as empirical evidence for incident metrics.
Relevance Score: Medium — adjacent conceptual review of agentic/multi-agent copilot architectures and tooling, but it contains no MTTD/MTTR, incident-response, or AIOps measurements.

Title: A Research Landscape of Agentic AI and Large Language Models: Applications, Challenges and Future Directions
Authors: Sarfraz Brohi; Qurat-ul-ain Mastoi; N. Z. Jhanjhi; Thulasyammal Ramiah Pillai
Year & Venue: 2025; Algorithms (MDPI journal), vol. 18, article 499; Received 1 July 2025, Published 11 August 2025
Core Problem Addressed: A notable lack of peer-reviewed research at the intersection of LLMs and Agentic AI: no existing study brings together the conceptual, technical, and ethical aspects of both in a single coherent analysis, including how LLM challenges (security, privacy, trust, bias, misinformation, energy, value alignment, transparency) propagate into autonomous Agentic AI systems (Sec. 1, p. 4)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: No system is built; the paper proposes a unified forward-looking research landscape. It frames Agentic AI as LLM-powered: the LLM is the reasoning core handling instruction decomposition and dialogue via an orchestrator layer, while specialised agents (e.g., search, filtering, booking) act through an External Services Layer of APIs and tools (Sec. 1, Fig. 3, p. 3). It maps eight Agentic AI challenges to research directions: Trustworthy, Aligned, Explainable, Collaborative, Memory-Aware, Cooperative, Safe, and Accountable Agents (Sec. 5, Table 2, p. 22), plus human-in-the-loop mechanisms and mixed-initiative control for oversight (Sec. 5.4, p. 23)
Methodology: Structured scoping review with thematic analysis (not a formal systematic review), four-phase method: search of Google Scholar, Scopus, and arXiv (English, 2020-2025) yielding 327 documents (142 Google Scholar, 110 Scopus, 75 arXiv), screened to 71 papers plus 13 manual sources = 84 final sources; deduplication in Zotero; keyword co-occurrence analysis with VOSviewer 1.6.20 (Sec. 2, pp. 5-8). Complemented by small-scale illustrative demonstrations of bias and cultural inclusivity using GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1: three rephrased prompts per issue, per model, on three different days, via public web interfaces with default settings (Sec. 4, pp. 12-13)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable (no MTTD/MTTR measurements; landscape review). Qualitative claims only: in cybersecurity, agents can "rapidly assess the situation, prioritise risks, and execute containment and remediation actions" minimising operational disruption, and firms such as ReliaQuest and CrowdStrike deploy Agentic AI to automate SOC tasks, enhance accuracy, and accelerate response times (Sec. 3.3, p. 10); in customer service, Agentic AI systems "cut down response times" (Sec. 3.6, p. 12)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Identifies that LLM challenges (security/privacy/trust, misinformation/misuse/bias, energy, value misalignment, explainability) propagate and intensify inside Agentic AI, and adds eight Agentic-specific challenges: security/privacy/trust, goal misalignment, opaque decision-making, limited human oversight, context management, multi-agent coordination, long-term safety, ethical/legal accountability (Secs. 4-5, Tables 1-2, pp. 12, 22). Notes coordination failure modes from incomplete information and governance gaps (Sec. 5.6, p. 24), behavioural drift and error accumulation over time (Sec. 5.7, p. 24), extra energy demands of coordinating multiple agents (Sec. 4.3, p. 17), and reports Med-Flamingo achieving "up to a 20% improvement in diagnostic accuracy compared to prior models" (Sec. 3.2, p. 10); bias demos show consistent divergence between ChatGPT and DeepSeek outputs (Sec. 4.2, pp. 14-15)
Limitations / Future Work: Authors state the scoping review "was not based on a formal systematic review framework"; future reviews should adopt protocol-based reviews, meta-analyses and systematic reviews as the literature matures (Sec. 6, p. 25). The GPT-4o/DeepSeek-R1 demonstrations are "not intended to be rigorous or fully reproducible" and are illustrative, not formal experiments (Sec. 4, pp. 12-13). Future research roadmap: trustworthy/secure agent architectures (sandboxing, scoped credentials), value alignment via inverse reinforcement learning and human feedback, explainable autonomy, mixed-initiative human oversight, persistent memory architectures, scalable multi-agent coordination protocols, long-term safety benchmarks and runtime monitoring, and accountability protocols with audit trails (Sec. 5, Table 2, pp. 21-25)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper supplies conceptual scaffolding rather than incident-response evidence. Its LLM-as-reasoning-core plus orchestrator plus tool-using-agents architecture (Fig. 3) mirrors the copilot design an MTTD/MTTR-reduction agent would need, and its cybersecurity section documents real SOC deployments (ReliaQuest, CrowdStrike) where Agentic AI accelerates detection and response, directly adjacent to incident management. The eight Agentic AI challenges, especially limited human oversight, opaque decision-making, context management, and multi-agent coordination, enumerate the risks a thesis copilot must mitigate to be trusted in production incident response. Its human-in-the-loop and collaborative-agent research directions can justify the copilot (rather than fully autonomous) framing of my research. However, it provides no AIOps datasets or MTTD/MTTR baselines, so it serves as background and challenge taxonomy, not as empirical support
Relevance Score: Medium — an adjacent landscape review of Agentic AI/multi-agent challenges with qualitative SOC response-time claims, but no measurement of MTTD/MTTR or incident-management metrics

Title: LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems for Software Engineering: Literature Review, Vision and the Road Ahead
Authors: Junda He; Christoph Treude; David Lo
Year & Venue: 2025; arXiv preprint (arXiv:2404.04834v4, 18 Jul 2025), formatted as an ACM article with placeholder DOI (10.1145/nnnnnnn); ⚠ Ambiguous: final publication venue not identified in the PDF
Core Problem Addressed: Single LLM-based agents are limited because real-world software engineering problems span multiple domains and require expertise from various fields; the paper targets the lack of a systematic mapping of LLM-Based Multi-Agent (LMA) systems across the software development lifecycle and the absence of a structured research agenda for autonomous, scalable, trustworthy LMA systems (Sec. 1, pp. 1-3)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Defines an LMA system as an orchestration platform plus LLM-based agents: coordination models (cooperative, competitive, hierarchical, mixed), communication mechanisms (centralized, decentralized, hierarchical), and planning styles (CPDE/DPDE) (Sec. 2.3, p. 4); catalogs recurring agent roles for code generation — Orchestrator, Programmer, Reviewer, Tester, Information Retriever — with iterative feedback loops (Sec. 3.2, pp. 6-7); reviews frameworks such as ChatDev, MetaGPT, AgileCoder (Waterfall/Agile process emulation) and human-in-the-loop designs (AISD, MARE) (Sec. 3.5, pp. 9-10; Sec. 5.2.1, p. 17); proposes a two-phase research agenda: enhancing individual agent capabilities and optimizing agent synergy (Sec. 5, pp. 12-22)
Methodology: Systematic literature review (Kitchenham-style with inclusion/exclusion criteria): keyword search on DBLP conducted November 14th, 2024, yielding 41 primary studies, plus backward/forward snowballing to transitive closure adding 30 papers, totaling 71 primary studies (Sec. 3, pp. 5-6); complemented by two case studies using ChatDev (agents powered by GPT-3.5-turbo, temperature 0.2) to autonomously develop Snake and Tetris games (Sec. 4, p. 10)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable (literature review and vision paper; no MTTD, MTTR, alert fatigue, or incident resolution time metrics are reported); the closest reviewed works are RCAgent, which "performs root cause analysis in cloud environments" by collecting system data, analyzing logs, and diagnosing issues, and AgentFL for three-phase fault localization, but no incident metrics are given (Sec. 3.3, p. 8)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Case studies: ChatDev produced a fully functional Snake game on the second attempt, averaging 76 seconds and $0.019 per attempt; for Tetris it succeeded only on the tenth attempt, still lacking row-removal functionality, averaging 70 seconds and $0.020 per attempt — showing efficiency and low cost but limits "in handling more complex tasks that require deeper logical reasoning and abstraction" (Sec. 4, pp. 11-12); LMA systems are argued superior to Mixture of Experts because agents communicate, integrate external tool feedback (compilers, static analyzers, testing frameworks), and support continuous human-in-the-loop collaboration (Sec. 6.1, p. 22)
Limitations / Future Work: Threat to validity: possible inadvertent exclusion of relevant studies during search/selection, mitigated via DBLP coverage and snowballing (Sec. 6.2, p. 22); identified gaps: general-purpose LLMs lack nuanced SE expertise for specialized roles, human-centered prompting frameworks, underexplored human-agent task allocation, benchmarks that ignore collaboration, scaling bottlenecks (communication overload, memory limits, conflicting shared information), static architectures lacking dynamic adaptation, and unresolved privacy/partial-information sharing across organizations (Sec. 5, pp. 13-22); future work: specialized datasets and pre-training for SE roles, advanced prompting strategies, human-agent task allocation, scalable methodologies, and data access control (Sec. 7, p. 23)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper supplies a reusable architectural vocabulary for my agentic-copilot design: the orchestration platform taxonomy (coordination models, communication topologies, CPDE/DPDE planning) and the Orchestrator/Programmer/Reviewer/Tester role pattern map directly onto multi-agent incident-response pipelines for detection, diagnosis, and remediation. Its coverage of RCAgent (cloud root cause analysis) and AgentFL (fault localization) identifies concrete LMA precedents for reducing MTTD/MTTR, even though the review itself reports no incident metrics. The research agenda on human-agent task allocation, human-in-the-loop intervention points, and collaboration-aware evaluation benchmarks informs how I should design and evaluate a copilot that keeps SRE operators in the loop. Finally, its case-study evidence on cost, latency, and failure modes of LMA systems grounds expectations about orchestration overhead in production incident scenarios.
Relevance Score: Medium — adjacent work: it provides LMA architecture patterns and reviews root-cause-analysis/fault-localization agents relevant to incident response, but it is SE-lifecycle-focused and measures no MTTD/MTTR metrics.

Title: A Survey of AIOps in the Era of Large Language Models
Authors: Lingzhe Zhang; Tong Jia; Mengxi Jia; Yifan Wu; Aiwei Liu; Yong Yang; Zhonghai Wu; Xuming Hu; Philip S. Yu; Ying Li
Year & Venue: ⚠ Ambiguous: 2025; typeset as Journal of the ACM (J. ACM), Vol. 37, No. 4, Article 111, August 2025, but the DOI is a placeholder and the copy is the arXiv preprint arXiv:2507.12472 [cs.SE]
Core Problem Addressed: A comprehensive understanding of the impact, potential, and limitations of LLMs in AIOps "remains in its infancy"; traditional ML/DL AIOps suffers from complex feature engineering, lack of cross-platform generality, lack of cross-task flexibility, limited adaptability, and restricted automation levels for runtime failure management in large-scale distributed systems (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 1.1, pp. 2-3)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Not a system but a survey organized around 4 RQs: RQ1 data sources (system-generated metrics/logs/traces plus new human-generated software information, source code, QA, incident reports); RQ2 evolved task pipeline (Failure Perception -> Root Cause Analysis -> Assisted Remediation, with new LLM-era tasks such as root cause report generation, script generation, automatic execution); RQ3 five method families (foundation model, fine-tuning, embedding-based, prompt-based, knowledge-based incl. RAG and Tool-Augmented Generation); RQ4 evaluation. Agentic AI appears via tool-augmented LLM agents, e.g., RCAgent, RCACopilot, a GPT-based agent using 150 tools to manage Linux servers, LLexus, and AIOpsLab's agent-cloud interface; a 5-level automation taxonomy (Assisted Questioning -> Mitigation Solution Generation -> Command Recommendation -> Script Generation -> Automatic Execution) frames human-in-the-loop vs. autonomous remediation (Sec. 1.3, p. 4; Sec. 3-4, pp. 6-15; Sec. 5.5, pp. 20-21)
Methodology: Systematic literature review with a defined protocol (search strategy, inclusion criteria IC1-IC4, exclusion criteria EC1-EC5) over 5 databases (Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM DL, arXiv), papers after 2020: 761 retrieved, 614 after deduplication, 395 full-text reviews, 163 studies meeting inclusion criteria; ⚠ Ambiguous: the abstract states "183 research papers published between January 2020 and December 2024" while Sec. 2.3/Fig. 4 report 163 selected studies; automation levels additionally refined via interviews with on-call engineers from partner companies (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 2, pp. 5-6; Sec. 4.3, pp. 14-15)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified — no quantitative MTTD/MTTR/alert-fatigue values are reported; only qualitative claims, e.g., Automatic Execution "significantly speeding up resolution time and reducing the workload on operations personnel" and Command Recommendation "shortening the repair time"; surveyed evaluation metrics are classification, generation, execution-success, and manual metrics, none time-to-detect/recover (Sec. 4.3, p. 15; Sec. 6.1, pp. 21-23)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Tool-Augmented Generation lets LLMs query monitoring systems, execute diagnostic scripts, and automate workflows (RCAgent, RCACopilot, LLexus, AIOpsLab, a GPT-4 agent "competently using 150 distinct tools across nine categories"); however, for the highest automation level (Automatic Execution) "related work is limited, and its practical effectiveness remains to be verified"; LLM computational overhead is critical for continuous failure perception (e.g., inference must complete within 1 second for a 10-second detection window) and no LLM-based work has adequately addressed it (Sec. 4.3, p. 15; Sec. 5.5, pp. 20-21; Sec. 7.1, pp. 24-25)
Limitations / Future Work: Four open challenges: (1) time-efficiency and cost-effectiveness of LLM-based AIOps (inference cost may make small models + OCEs preferable); (2) deeper use of diverse failure data — "no current work has effectively incorporated traces data" and incident-report-driven RCA "disrupts the automation flow of AIOps"; (3) generalizability and model adaptability under software evolution lack empirical validation; (4) integration with existing AIOps toolchains and smaller models rather than building entirely new methods (Sec. 7, pp. 24-26)
Relevance to My Thesis: This survey is a foundational map for the thesis: its Failure Perception -> Root Cause Analysis -> Assisted Remediation pipeline aligns directly with the MTTD (detection) and MTTR (diagnosis + remediation) phases of incident response. The five-level automation taxonomy gives a ready framework for positioning an Agentic AI copilot on the human-in-the-loop spectrum, and its catalog of agentic systems (RCACopilot, RCAgent, AIOpsLab, LLexus) identifies concrete baselines and benchmarks. Critically, it shows that surveyed evaluations use classification/generation/execution metrics rather than MTTD/MTTR, exposing exactly the measurement gap the thesis targets. Its challenges on inference latency, cost, and toolchain integration also inform the copilot's design constraints.
Relevance Score: Medium — a comprehensive LLM4AIOps survey covering the full incident lifecycle and agentic tool-augmented approaches, but it does not itself measure MTTD/MTTR

Title: Agentic AI: A Comprehensive Survey of Technologies, Applications, and Societal Implications
Authors: Ashis Kumar Pati
Core Problem Addressed: A "striking lack of readily available and understandable materials" on agentic AI: foundational concepts are scattered across RL, human-AI collaboration, and LLM-based agent frameworks, with no comprehensive resource unifying them; existing surveys show gaps in traditional-AI vs agentic-AI distinctions, methodologies, agent types, societal impact, and open problems (Sec. II and II.A, pp. 151825-151827)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: No new architecture; a conceptual/structured survey. Defines agentic AI (proactivity; autonomy, adaptability, goal-directedness), distinguishes it from traditional AI and from AI agents (agents as bricks, agentic AI as the orchestrating house), presents a four-phase working loop (data collection, decision-making, learning, collaboration), classifies agents (reflex, model-based, goal-based, utility-based, learning, meta-reasoning; single-agent, multi-agent, swarm, human-AI collaborative), and reviews enabling technologies (LLMs/NLP, RL/IRL, imitation learning, MAS/swarm frameworks, neurosymbolic integration, knowledge graphs) and design frameworks (BDI, SOAR, ACT-R) plus simulation environments (Unity ML, OpenAI Gym, Mesa) (Sec. I.A-B, III, IV, pp. 151824-151830)
Methodology: Narrative literature survey/review (author calls it a "structured literature review"); compares itself with 11 existing surveys on coverage dimensions (BC/ID/ND scale, Table 3); no systematic search protocol, dataset, experiment, or sample size reported (Sec. II and II.A, Table 3, pp. 151825-151827)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable (conceptual survey; no MTTD, MTTR, alert-fatigue, or resolution-time metrics measured). Closest reported secondary data: citing [2], agentic AI across ~500 organisations showed "a 34.2% reduction in completing the task, increasing the accuracy by 7.7%" and 13.6% improved resource utilisation (Sec. I.A, p. 151825); qualitatively, IT & cybersecurity agents continuously monitor, detect threats, immediately block fraudulent transactions, and alert security systems (Sec. V.D, pp. 151831-151832)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Qualitative only: MAS enable hierarchical or peer-to-peer coordination for complex tasks (e.g., supply chains) and swarm systems suit dynamic environments (Sec. III.C, pp. 151828-151829); proposed evaluation metrics are robustness, scalability, safety, task completion rate, and communication efficiency (bandwidth/latency) (Sec. IV.B.3, p. 151830); reported failure modes include computational and coordination complexity as agent counts grow, black-box interpretability, unclear blame attribution among agents in a MAS, and security vulnerabilities from autonomy and direct database access (Sec. VII.A, pp. 151832-151833)
Limitations / Future Work: Open problems listed by the author: transparent/causal agentic AI, neuro-symbolic hybrid agents, multi-agent cooperation and negotiation, human-AI collaboration adapting to feedback and emotion, energy-efficient architectures, Sim2Real transfer, quantum computing for scalability, and robustness against adversarial attacks; also notes RL policies do not transfer across dissimilar domains and that hybrid human-oversight workflows and XAI are needed (Sec. V.D end, p. 151832; Sec. VII.B, pp. 151833-151834). The paper does not explicitly state limitations of its own survey method (Not specified)
Relevance to My Thesis: This survey supplies conceptual scaffolding rather than incident-response evidence. Its AI-agents-vs-agentic-AI distinction and orchestration framing (specialised agents coordinated into a goal-driven pipeline, with one agent alerting humans) map directly onto a copilot architecture for incident detection and remediation. The four-phase loop (perceive, decide, learn, collaborate) and the human-AI collaborative paradigm with hybrid oversight workflows support the human-in-the-loop copilot design in my thesis. Its proposed evaluation dimensions (robustness, task completion rate, communication latency) and its MAS failure modes (coordination overhead, blame attribution, interpretability) inform threats to validity when measuring MTTD/MTTR with agentic systems. However, it offers no AIOps, observability, or incident-metric evidence, so it serves only as background/definitional support.
Relevance Score: Low - a broad conceptual survey of agentic AI with a brief cybersecurity monitoring mention, but no AIOps/observability focus and no MTTD/MTTR or incident-resolution measurements.

Title: Artificial Empathy: A New Perspective for Analyzing and Designing Multi-Agent Systems
Authors: Jize Chen; Dali Zhang; Zhenshen Qu; Changhong Wang
Core Problem Addressed: Traditional consensus-based multi-agent collaboration only imitates biological synergy for state consistency and lacks a more fundamental cooperative mechanism covering both cooperation and competition; prior artificial empathy models ignore how agents' characteristics map to the degree of empathy and cannot elicit behaviors such as helping, altruism, and a sense of fairness (Sec. I, pp. 183649-183650)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Introduces an analytical model of empathy for multi-agent systems: empathy is abstracted as an optimization problem solved by minimizing Gibbs free energy (F = E - TH), yielding a Gibbs-distribution empathetic transfer matrix; two temperatures (T1 on empathetic utility, T2 on empathy entropy) define four agent modes — collective, equal, oligarchic, and monopolistic (Theorems 1-4); an adversarial bandit algorithm, Empathy-based Interactive Learner (EIL), integrates empathetic utility and empathy entropy into an integrated utility with a soft-max policy and adaptive coldness update driven by income entropy and policy entropy; no LLMs, copilots, or human-in-the-loop design are involved (Sec. III-IV, pp. 183652-183657)
Methodology: Theoretical modeling (free-energy optimization, four mode theorems with proofs) plus simulation experiments: EIL tested in four games — iterated prisoner's dilemma (T=5, R=3, P=1, S=0), ultimatum game (total resources r=10), 4-player ultimatum game, and a survival game with 2 strong and 2 weak agents; comparisons against Q-learning and multi-step agents; shared parameters b=e, alpha=0.001, L=500, w=100, mu in [0.0001, 200]; results averaged over 50 episodes of training (Sec. V, pp. 183658-183662)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable; the paper is a theoretical/simulation study on game-theoretic cooperation and reports no MTTD, MTTR, alert-fatigue, or incident-resolution measurements (Sec. V, pp. 183658-183662)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: EIL-agents in equal mode progressively converged to cooperation in the iterated prisoner's dilemma while two QL-agents converged to mutual defection; in the ultimatum game EIL converged to absolute fairness (5-5) versus (9-1) for QL — the external Nash equilibrium is transferred to a fairness equilibrium of integrated utility; EIL switched from exploration to exploitation more rapidly than QL; agents filtered out environmental pulses narrower than window w=100 and sensed wider ones (Property 1); varying (T1, T2) switched agents among equality, oligopoly, and monopoly patterns, and in the survival game strong-weak teams formed at (T1=19, T2=1), reducing power gaps (Sec. V, Figs. 6-10, pp. 183658-183662)
Limitations / Future Work: Behavior in more complex forms is also dominated by the environment, which is not yet modeled; future work will "explain the evolutionary patterns of the behavior under different external constraints of the environment" and build a systematic collaboration theory including collaboration model design, collaboration index analysis, and collaboration algorithm optimization (Sec. VI, p. 183663)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper is far from incident response: it contributes a bio-inspired mechanism (artificial empathy via free-energy optimization) for regulating cooperation and competition among learning agents, with no LLMs, copilots, observability, or AIOps context. Its indirect value for the thesis lies in the design of intrinsic utility shaping and temperature-controlled agent modes, which could inform how roles and cooperation incentives are balanced in a multi-agent incident-response copilot (e.g., detection vs. remediation agents sharing rewards). The adaptive entropy-based mechanism for sensing environment fluctuations is loosely analogous to anomaly-detection sensitivity tuning. However, it provides no metrics, architectures, or evaluations transferable to MTTD/MTTR reduction, so it serves at most as background on multi-agent coordination mechanisms.
Relevance Score: Low; the paper neither addresses IT operations, incident response, nor MTTD/MTTR, offering only tangential multi-agent cooperation-mechanism insights

Title: AI Agents vs. Agentic AI: A Conceptual taxonomy, applications and challenges

Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: A structured conceptual taxonomy separating AI Agents (modular, single-entity, LLM/LIM-driven, tool-augmented systems for narrow task automation) from Agentic AI (orchestrated multi-agent ecosystems with goal decomposition, dynamic role assignment, persistent episodic/semantic/vector memory, and coordinated autonomy) (Sec. 3.0.1-3.1, pp. 7-13). Architectural analysis covers perception/reasoning/action/learning modules for AI Agents and enhancements for Agentic AI: ensembles of specialized agents, advanced reasoning/planning (ReAct, CoT, Tree of Thoughts), persistent memory, and orchestration layers/meta-agents, with examples from AutoGPT, LangChain, AutoGen, CrewAI, MetaGPT, and ChatDev (Sec. 3.1.1-3.1.2, pp. 10-13). Methodology: Literature review (conceptual/taxonomic survey); a hybrid search methodology querying twelve platforms: academic databases (Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, arXiv) and AI-powered interfaces (ChatGPT, Perplexity.ai, DeepSeek, Hugging Face Search, Grok), using Boolean combinations of terms such as "AI Agents", "Agentic AI", "LLM Agents", "Tool-augmented LLMs", "Multi-Agent AI Systems" (Sec. 1.1.1, p. 4). Inclusion based on novelty, empirical evaluation, architectural contribution, and citation impact; the authors explicitly adopt a sequential, layered structure "[r]ather than organizing the study around formal research questions" (Sec. 1, p. 2; Sec. 1.1, p. 3). Number of papers included: Not specified. No dataset, experiment, or deployment reported.
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable (conceptual review; no MTTD/MTTR measurements or baselines reported). Qualitative claims relevant to incident response: in an enterprise cybersecurity incident response example, the agentic model "enhances decision latency, reduces false positives, and supports proactive threat containment" versus rule-based systems (Sec. 4.0.2, p. 16); in ICU decision support, coordinated agents are described as "reducing cognitive load, shortening decision times, and minimizing oversight risks" (Sec. 4.0.2, p. 16); email-triage AI Agents "reduce cognitive overload" (Sec. 4.0.1, pp. 13-14). Table 11 lists Atera AI Copilot for IT Operations, which "Diagnoses/resolves IT issues, automates ticketing, and learns from evolving infrastructures" (Table 11, p. 19). No quantitative figures are given for any of these claims.
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Provides a multi-dimensional comparative framework (Tables 1-9) distinguishing Generative AI, AI Agents, Agentic AI, and Generative Agents across autonomy, memory, orchestration, and coordination (Sec. 3.0.2, pp. 8-12). Documents Agentic AI failure modes: amplified causality deficits and inter-agent error cascades, communication/coordination bottlenecks, emergent behavior and instability (infinite planning loops, deadlocks), scalability and debugging complexity, compounded opacity in trust/explainability/verification, expanded adversarial attack surface (single point of compromise), and ethical/governance accountability gaps (Sec. 5.0.2, pp. 20-21). Also notes AI Agent computational cost and latency because each decision cycle "may require several LLM invocations" (Sec. 5.0.1, p. 17). No quantitative efficacy, overhead, or cost measurements are reported.
Limitations / Future Work: Authors acknowledge field-wide limitations: overreliance on hallucination-prone LLMs lacking causal reasoning; non-standardized orchestration protocols hindering interoperability and reproducibility; and that "many benchmark evaluations for agentic systems rely on artificial environments" while frameworks emphasize "architectural novelty over rigorous empirical validation" (Sec. 5.1, p. 22). Real-world Agentic AI implementations in healthcare are "still lacking due to the nascent nature of the field" (Sec. 4.0.2, p. 16). Future roadmap: proactive intelligence, tool integration, causal reasoning, continual learning, and trust/safety for AI Agents; multi-agent scaling, unified orchestration, persistent memory, simulation planning, ethical governance, and domain-specific systems for Agentic AI, plus the Absolute Zero (AZR) self-play learning paradigm (Sec. 6.2, pp. 24-25). No explicit section on the review's own methodological limitations (Not specified).
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper supplies the core conceptual vocabulary for the thesis: it formally separates single-entity AI Agents from orchestrated Agentic AI, a distinction needed to position an incident-response copilot on the autonomy spectrum. Its cybersecurity incident response use case (threat classification, log correlation, compliance, and mitigation agents under a central orchestrator with human analysts in the loop) is a direct architectural template for an MTTD/MTTR-reduction copilot in SRE/AIOps contexts. The catalog of Agentic AI failure modes (error cascades, coordination bottlenecks, emergent instability) and the ten mitigation mechanisms (RAG, ReAct loops, orchestration, auditing pipelines) can inform both the design and the threat-to-validity discussion of the thesis prototype. However, it offers no incident metrics, so it serves as taxonomic and architectural grounding rather than empirical evidence of MTTD/MTTR impact.
Relevance Score: Medium; it is a foundational Agentic AI / multi-agent taxonomy with an incident-response application example, but it is purely conceptual and reports no MTTD/MTTR or other incident metrics.

Title: Co-Evolving Multi-Agent Transfer Reinforcement Learning via Scenario Independent Representation
Authors: Ayesha Siddiqua; Siming Liu; Ayesha Siddika Nipu; Anthony Harris; Yan Liu
Core Problem Addressed: Not an IT-operations paper: it targets the difficulty of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) in Multi-Agent Systems, where learning complex cooperative/competitive tasks from scratch is "challenging and often unfeasible" for large numbers of agents due to exponential state expansion, scenario-dependent state sizes that block knowledge transfer, and static built-in AI opponents that cap further policy improvement (Abstract; Sec. I, pp. 99439-99440).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Co-MACTRL: a co-evolutionary curriculum transfer learning framework for MARL (no LLMs, no copilot, no human-in-the-loop). Uses scenario-independent state/action representations via Agent Influence Maps (64x64 Multi-Agent Influence Map for abstracted global info; 37x37 local IM) feeding fixed-size A3C actor-critic MLPs (two hidden layers of 64 neurons) under Centralized Training with Semi-Centralized Execution (CTSCE); attack action generalized to the closest enemy. Curriculum sequence 3m -> 8m -> 2s3z -> 3s5z, then an arena of three MARL learners co-evolving against static built-in AI and each other on multi-player enabled SMAC (MP-SMAC, map 3s5z_mp) (Sec. III-A to III-D, pp. 99442-99446; Algorithms 1-2).
Methodology: Simulation-based controlled experiments in the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) and the authors' extended MP-SMAC (StarCraft II). Results collected from 7 different random seeds, experiments up to 80 million steps, evaluation every 25 game episodes; CTL uses 1M steps per map; evaluation matrix runs 32 distinct game episodes per map per phase; Co-MACTRL trained 72M game steps over four cycles with three learners; compared against baseline MARL (3s5z from scratch) and Co-MARL without CTL (Sec. III-B.2, p. 99444; Sec. III-D, pp. 99445-99446; Sec. IV-A/B, pp. 99447-99449).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable — a game-based MARL study; no MTTD, MTTR, alert fatigue, or incident-resolution metrics are reported anywhere in the paper (entire paper; results are win rates in StarCraft II scenarios, Sec. IV, pp. 99446-99449).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: MACTRL (CTL) learner reached 87% win rate on 3m, 68% on 8m, 85% on 2s3z, and 85% early on 3s5z vs. 72% for the regular learner in 8M steps; "the MACTRL learner outperforms regular MARL learner by an average of 50% across all four scenarios"; highest average win rate 80%. Co-MACTRL learners surpass MACTRL peak values by nearly 7%; over cycles, 3m win rate rose 80%->90% and 8m 60%->73%; Co-MARL without CTL averaged nearly 50% lower on unseen maps. Failure mode: continued training on 3s5z degrades performance on earlier maps after 7M steps (forgetting); learners exhibit an emergent generalized "focus fire" strategy (Sec. IV-A/B/C, Tables 2-3, Figs. 4-6, pp. 99446-99449).
Limitations / Future Work: Authors state testing "was confined to a restricted set of scenarios"; future work: evaluate on a broader spectrum of heterogeneous environments with more intricate maps, explore more advanced curriculum learning designs and knowledge transfer approaches for co-evolutionary MARL, and integrate additional deep RL techniques such as recurrent neural networks (Sec. V, p. 99450).
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper is tangential to Agentic AI copilots for incident response: it contains no LLMs, observability, AIOps, or incident metrics. Its value to the thesis is conceptual — it demonstrates multi-agent coordination mechanisms (shared reward, centralized training with abstracted global state) and shows that curriculum transfer and co-evolution let agent teams reuse knowledge across scenarios instead of learning from scratch, a principle analogous to transferring incident-handling knowledge across incident types. The scenario-independent state representation idea could inform how an incident-response agent normalizes heterogeneous telemetry into a fixed input. The reported forgetting when training shifts to new scenarios is a cautionary finding for continuously learning ops agents. Overall it can only support background discussion of multi-agent learning, not the MTTD/MTTR evidence base.
Relevance Score: Low — a game-based MARL/transfer-learning study with no incident response, AIOps, LLM, or MTTD/MTTR content; only tangentially relevant as multi-agent systems background.

Title: The Rise of Agentic AI: A Review of Definitions, Frameworks, Architectures, Applications, Evaluation Metrics, and Challenges

Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable (review paper; MTTD/MTTR are never measured or named). Only adjacent number: Task Completion Time for LangGraph, Autogen, GoEX "averaged 12 ± 2 min TCT, which is a 34.2% improvement against traditional AI" (Sec. 3.6.2, p. 37).

Reported figures: LangGraph and CrewAI "show around 94% accuracy in complex task execution"; Claude 3.5/LLaMa-3.2 96% accuracy with plan caching; ~94% rule fidelity for neuro-symbolic agents; ECG AI 96-97% accuracy (Sec. 3.6.2, pp. 36-38). Relevance to My Thesis: This review supplies the conceptual backbone for the thesis: precise definitions separating AI agents, agentic AI, MAS, GenAI, and autonomic computing, plus five architectural models (ReAct, supervisor/hierarchical, hybrid, BDI, neuro-symbolic) that can frame the design of an incident-response copilot. Relevance Score: Medium - a broad, high-quality taxonomy/architecture reference that touches autonomous IT operations, incident response, and evaluation metrics, but provides no MTTD/MTTR measurement or incident-management experiment.

Title: Agent System Mining: Vision, Benefits, and Challenges
Authors: Andrei Tour; Artem Polyvyanyy; Anna Kalenkova
Year & Venue: 2021; IEEE Access, vol. 9 (received June 16, 2021; published July 8, 2021)
Core Problem Addressed: Process Mining techniques make simplifying assumptions about business processes, and relaxing these assumptions yields more realistic process models that are "often difficult to visualize and, consequently, to understand" — the "spaghetti process models" problem; manual design and update of process models also take significant time and effort (Sec. I, pp. 99480-99481).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Proposes Agent System Mining (ASM), combining Process Mining with Agent-Based Modeling (ABM) to automatically infer Multi-Agent System (MAS) models of operational business processes from real-world event data; macro-level process behavior emerges bottom-up from micro-level autonomous agent interactions instead of a centralized control flow; the ASM Framework maps activities to a V-model MAS modeling lifecycle with five phases (Motivate, Plan, Develop, Evaluate, Use) and seven ASM activities (search, project, discover, enhance, integrate, diagnose, check); Phases 1 and 5 are manual (human modelers/BPM stakeholders), while ASM algorithms partially or fully automate Phases 2-4; no LLMs or copilot design are involved (Sec. IV, Figs. 6-7, pp. 99485-99488).
Methodology: Vision/conceptual position paper: (1) a motivating example of an "order fulfillment" retail process using GIS data from the AnyLogic "Supply Chain GIS Model", with DFM models discovered by the Disco tool and a MAS simulation in AnyLogic (Sec. II, pp. 99481-99483); (2) a structured literature review following vom Brocke et al. and Cooper's taxonomy: queries on Scopus and Web of Science (executed 16 February 2021, publications >= 2010) returned 2,094 merged publications, filtered to 149 relevant papers analyzed against 3 research questions (Sec. V, pp. 99490-99491); no empirical evaluation, prototype deployment, or controlled experiment is reported.
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable — the paper reports no incident-response metrics (MTTD, MTTR, alert fatigue, or resolution time); the closest qualitative claim is that automation yields "shorter model development cycles" so "organizations can react faster and take timely actions to resolve arising issues" (Sec. IV-C, pp. 99488-99489).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Argues MAS models mitigate "spaghetti process models" because MAS behavior complexity can grow over time "while the size and complexity of the model stay unchanged"; direct benefits: evidence-based modeling, shorter model development cycles, better conformance; indirect benefits: managing complex, flexible, and context-aware processes; identifies 8 challenges: MAS metamodel selection, model scope definition, simulation/static analysis support, model validation, event data selection, agent type discovery, sub-model discovery, and modeling language selection; the review concludes existing works "do not allow, neither individually nor collectively, implementing the ASM framework" (Sec. IV-C, IV-D, Sec. V-C2, pp. 99488-99492).
Limitations / Future Work: The proposal is a vision without implemented ASM algorithms or empirical validation; future research organized around three areas: metamodels/formalisms for representing MAS models discovered from business process data, ASM algorithms for discovering and enhancing executable MAS models, and techniques for assessing the quality of discovered MAS models; further analysis of ASM benefits across application domains and industry sectors is needed to validate the ASM Framework (Sec. VI, p. 99492).
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper is grounded in BPM/Process Mining, not IT operations or incident response, and predates LLM-based agentic copilots. Its value to the thesis is conceptual: it formalizes how multi-agent models can be discovered from event logs and how micro-level agent behaviors produce emergent macro-level system behavior, a framing that parallels mining incident timelines and observability event data to model on-call/automation agents. Its lifecycle framework (discover, enhance, integrate, diagnose, check) and its challenges (agent type discovery, event data selection, model validation) offer transferable vocabulary for designing and validating an agentic AIOps pipeline. However, it contributes no incident metrics, no LLM techniques, and no copilot architecture, so it can only serve as background on MAS modeling foundations.
Relevance Score: Low — a conceptual BPM/process-mining vision paper with no AIOps, LLM, or MTTD/MTTR content; only tangentially relevant through its multi-agent modeling framework.

Title: LLM Agentic Workflow for Automated Vulnerability Detection and Remediation in Infrastructure-as-Code
Authors: Dheer Toprani; Vijay K. Madisetti

III-IV, pp. 69176-69178)
Methodology: Prototype implementation plus experimental evaluation on a curated corpus of 10 AWS CloudFormation templates (1-12 resources each), about half deliberately seeded with known misconfigurations (unencrypted S3, permissive IAM, open Security Groups, unencrypted RDS); ground-truth annotation by one AWS specialty-certified cloud engineer; compared conceptually against CDK-Nag and manual audits (Sec.
