III.B, p. 69177; Sec. V.A, V.D, pp. 69178-69179)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Multi-agent orchestration "enhances modularity, scalability, and maintainability" with independently improvable agents; RAG grounding reduced LLM hallucinations (deprecated parameters/outdated services); latency per template 80-100 s total (retrieval 1-3 s; LLM inference 15-40 s per step) vs under 5 s for static rule checks; ~5% of remediations were overly conservative; the LLM struggled with conditional/parameterized templates; knowledge-base staleness caused missed flags until updated (Sec. III.A, p. 69177; Sec. V.B-V.E, pp. 69178-69179)
Limitations / Future Work: Limitations: dependency on an up-to-date knowledge base (outdated entries cause false positives/missed issues); poor handling of conditional logic and specialized templates; small 10-template evaluation with manual annotation. Future work: developer feedback loop, organization-specific "context modules", hybrid rule-based prescreening before LLM invocation, generalization to Terraform and multi-cloud (Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes), ablation studies and semi-automated labeling to scale evaluation (Sec. V.A, p. 69178; Sec. VI-VII, pp. 69180-69181)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper demonstrates a concrete three-agent LLM pipeline (retrieval, detection, reporting) with RAG grounding that is architecturally transferable to an incident-response copilot: the detection agent parallels alert triage and the report agent parallels remediation-guidance generation for on-call engineers. Its evidence that RAG reduces hallucinations and false positives is directly useful for arguing that a grounded agentic copilot can lower alert fatigue. The reported latency profile (80-100 s per analysis) provides a benchmark for whether agentic pipelines fit time-critical MTTD/MTTR loops. However, it targets pre-deployment IaC security rather than live incident response, and it reports no MTTD/MTTR measurements, so it serves as supporting architectural evidence rather than direct metric evidence.
Relevance Score: Medium - adjacent work: a multi-agent LLM+RAG workflow for cloud operations security with detection-rate, false-positive, and latency metrics, but it addresses pre-deployment vulnerability detection and does not measure MTTD/MTTR or incident response.

Title: Small Language Model Agent for the Operations of Continuously Updating ICT Systems
Authors: Nobukazu Fukuda; Haruhisa Nozue; Haruo Oishi
Year & Venue: 2025; IEEE Access, vol. 13 (published 24 February 2025)
Core Problem Addressed: Management of ICT systems (networks, servers) is time-intensive and requires strict adherence to continuously updated operational manuals and policies; existing LLM agents presume sophisticated API-based proprietary LLMs, raising operational cost and confidentiality concerns, while SLMs perform significantly worse in decision-making tasks, fail to interpret context, and struggle with long-horizon trajectories (Sec. I, pp. 37522-37523).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: A single Small Language Model (SLM) agent framework for autonomous ICT operation deployable on one GPU, using few-shot prompting with two techniques: (A) nested thoughts — past trajectories are extended with subtask begin/end tags and decomposed into blocks with retrieval keys, timestamps, and Python script actions executed in the agent; (B) dynamic prompt reconfiguration — template-based block retrieval via log parsing (regular expressions), dynamic top-k cutoff, and diversity-aware exemplar selection to mitigate empirically identified shortcut reasoning; post-processing safety check rejects any output whose template is dissimilar to exemplar outputs, enforcing conformity to operational policies; the goal is given by the system operator and the agent interacts iteratively with the ICT system; SLMs used: quantized LLaMA2 (7B), Gemma2 (9B), Mistral (7B); similarity via all-mpnet-base-v2 SentenceTransformer (Sec. IV, pp. 37525-37527; Sec. V-C, p. 37528).
Methodology: Controlled experiments (prototype evaluation) on two benchmarks: ALFWorld, a public synthetic text-based benchmark with 134 environmental settings across 6 task types and 12 exemplar trajectories; and WideEnet, a real-world benchmark of wide-area Ethernet network operations built from operational manuals with 7 tasks, 34 exemplar trajectories, and 85 test environmental settings, plus incremental environmental updates (command format changes, added/deleted operations) with only two updated trajectories added; metric: task success rate; baselines: Act, ReAct, RAP; hardware: NVIDIA GeForce 2080Ti with 11GB memory (Sec. V-A to V-C, pp. 37528).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified — no MTTD, MTTR, alert fatigue, or resolution time metrics are reported; the paper qualitatively states autonomous operation "has the potential to reduce the time and burden of human endeavors" (Abstract, p. 37522) and that the SLM agent is expected to "mitigate the time-intensive endeavors of system operators" (Sec. VI, p. 37532).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: On ALFWorld, the proposed method with LLaMA2 reaches 96.3% success, outperforming ReAct with GPT-4 (85.8%) and RAP with GPT-4 (94.8%); shortcut-aware exemplar sampling raises two-shot success from 84.3% (unaware) to 96.3% vs 79.9% one-shot; on WideEnet, best success is Mistral (88.9%) and largest improvement is LLaMA2 (3.70% to 87.0%) over ReAct; under incremental updates, adding a few trajectories improves success from 29.4% to 78.8% after the third update; computational overhead: on average 5.2 times as many LM calls as environment steps and 2.1 times the LM calls of ReAct; a failure mode is shown where the SLM outputs an erroneous format and the safety check marks the task failed (Sec. V-D, pp. 37529-37531).
Limitations / Future Work: Limitations: the agent cannot handle situations not covered by the extended trajectories, and manually or heuristically augmenting thoughts/tags to operational histories is costly; some manuals are free-format with charts/diagrams, making mechanical trajectory generation a challenging problem; verification requires building an interactive environment, which demands extensive system knowledge and development effort. Future work: extracting agent-readable trajectories from multi-modal documents and operational histories, and constructing low-cost agent verification environments; the framework could extend to microservices, cloud, 5G/WAN, provisioning, root cause analysis, and troubleshooting (Sec. VI, p. 37532).
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper demonstrates a cost- and confidentiality-conscious agentic approach to autonomous ICT operations that directly informs the design of an incident-response copilot: its policy-conforming action generation and exemplar-similarity safety gate are concrete mechanisms for keeping an Agentic AI within approved runbooks, a key concern when automating remediation to reduce MTTR. Its evidence that a locally deployed SLM agent can outperform GPT-4-based ReAct/RAP supports on-premises copilot architectures for organizations with data-sensitivity constraints. The continuous-update adaptation results are relevant to real operations where runbooks evolve after incidents. However, it evaluates task success rate rather than MTTD/MTTR, so it supplies architectural and safety insights rather than incident-metric baselines for the thesis.
Relevance Score: Medium — an SLM/LLM agent for autonomous network/ICT operations (AIOps-adjacent, single-agent) with strong methodological relevance, but it does not measure MTTD, MTTR, or other incident-response metrics.

Title: ARM: Autonomous Remediation and Management With LLM Agents for Intent-Driven Control
Authors: Vasilis Avgerinos; Kostas Ramantas; Luis Alonso; Christos Verikoukis
Year & Venue: 2026 (published online 26 December 2025); IEEE Internet of Things Journal, vol. 13, no. 9
Core Problem Addressed: Growing complexity of cloud-native, edge, and IoT infrastructures makes manual configuration, fault remediation, and lifecycle management unsustainable, while rule-based or bespoke ML automation lacks adaptability and explainability (Abstract; Sec. I, p. 1). The authors also target a gap in current LLM-agent AIOps work: an "overwhelming focus on problem identification rather than autonomous mitigation", leaving recovery to manual intervention (Sec. II-C, p. 3).
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: ARM: a closed-loop, intent-driven framework where user-defined intents spawn Prometheus-based monitoring loops; on SLA violation a structured intent object triggers a single LLM agent (ReAct-influenced, round-based loop interleaving planning, tool invocation, and reasoning) that performs RCA and executes mitigations (pod rescheduling, scaling, configuration updates) via an MCP server exposing tools through an API (Abstract; Sec. III-D, p. 3; Sec. IV-A, p. 3-4). Tools are grouped in four categories (planning, Kubernetes, monitoring, utility); a system prompt enforces planning-first rules (create_action_plan first, replan on contradiction, terminate only after generate_operational_summary), evidence-first reasoning, action bias, and pattern-to-action heuristics; safeguards and human approval workflows can be configured per tool (Sec. IV-B and IV-C, p. 4-5). Agents are built on GPT-5 (primary) and GPT-5-mini (baseline) (Sec. VI, p. 7). The single-agent loop is chosen over multiagent/planner-executor designs for auditability (Sec. IV-A, p. 4).
Methodology: Prototype deployment with a systematic controlled fault-injection (chaos engineering) evaluation on a virtualized cloud-edge K3s Kubernetes cluster of seven QEMU-virtualized nodes across three zones (two cloud nodes 4 vCPU/4 GB, four edge nodes 2 vCPU/2 GB, one management node), with Prometheus/Grafana observability (Sec. V-A, p. 5). Synthetic IoT workloads generated with an extended MuBench framework for three applications: IoT Gateway (3 microservices), Smart Manufacturing (8 microservices), Smart City Traffic Management (12 microservices); 20 experiments per application yielding 60 fault scenarios covering pod-level (CPU, memory, pod disruption) and node-level (CPU/memory contention via chaosd) anomalies plus baseline controls (Sec. V-B and V-C, p. 5-6). Four-phase protocol (reset/warmup, baseline collection, chaos injection, agent recovery); recovery deemed successful if post-intervention metrics are within tolerance of baseline (epsilon = 0.15 for 95th-percentile latency, 0.01 for request success rate) (Sec. V-D and V-E, p. 6-7).
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: MTTD and MTTR are not reported by name, but detection/identification and resolution-time results are given: the agent "identifies SLA violations with 52.9% accuracy and mitigates 70.7% of them successfully" (Abstract, p. 1); the GPT-5 agent "restores SLA metrics in roughly 80% of fault injection runs" with correct identification "in about 78% of cases" (Sec. VII, p. 9). Wall-clock remediation time: GPT-5 typically faster than GPT-5-mini (e.g., 5.2 vs 12.8 min for IoT Gateway), except Smart City (11.8 vs 7.4 min) (Sec. VI-B, p. 8). Latency recovery metric Rlat: GPT-5 reclaimed 80.4% and GPT-5-mini 79.4% of CPU-stress-induced performance degradation despite moderate binary success (55.6% and 44.4%) (Sec. VI-A, p. 7). No human-operator or non-agentic baseline for detection or resolution time is reported (Not specified).
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Demonstrates feasibility of an LLM agent closing the full detect-diagnose-mitigate loop; claimed as the first LLM-driven agentic system that autonomously mitigates SLA violations via infrastructure-level actions in cloud-edge/IoT environments (Sec. I, p. 2). Model-size effects: GPT-5 needs fewer reasoning rounds for pod-level incidents (10.2-23.0 vs 27.7-34.2 for GPT-5-mini) and maintains >80% identification accuracy as topology complexity grows, while GPT-5-mini drops to 64.7% on the 12-service topology and fails to recognize the healthy baseline (0.0%) (Sec. VI-A and VI-B, p. 7-8). Tool-call analysis shows observability calls dominate over actuation, indicating a cautious, evidence-gathering agent; GPT-5-mini shows fragmented trial-and-error replanning (Sec. VI-C, p. 8-9). Authors argue scaling depends more on context compression and tooling optimization than on larger models (Sec. VI-B, p. 8); single-agent loop preferred over multiagent frameworks for auditability and explainability (Sec. IV-A, p. 4).
Limitations / Future Work: Acknowledged limitations: "nonnegligible wall-clock remediation times for the largest topology, and a distinct performance gap between model sizes", suggesting zero-touch control currently requires frontier-class models (Sec. VII, p. 9); binary success metric obscures partial recovery, and constrained emulated VMs sometimes make full return to baseline physically impossible (Sec. VI-A, p. 7); the smaller model's success can exceed its identification accuracy due to latent faults with little observable degradation (Sec. VI-A, p. 7-8). Future work: context-compression paradigms, deeper agent architectures with a more diverse tool set (including ML-based anomaly detection), fine-tuning smaller models, formalizing safety safeguards for high-impact actions, and deployment in larger, more heterogeneous real-world IoT testbeds (Sec. VII, p. 9).
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper is a near-direct instantiation of the thesis topic: an LLM agent that both detects SLA violations (proxy for MTTD) and autonomously remediates them (proxy for MTTR) in a Kubernetes observability stack, closing the AIOps loop that most prior work leaves at diagnosis. Its architecture (intent-triggered ReAct-style loop, MCP tool server over kubectl/Prometheus, planning-first prompt with configurable human-approval safeguards) provides a concrete design reference for a copilot-style incident-response agent. Its evaluation protocol (chaos injection, baseline-relative recovery criterion, identification accuracy, remediation success, wall-clock resolution time, reasoning rounds) offers reusable metrics even though MTTD/MTTR are not named explicitly. The single-agent vs model-size findings and the observability-dominated tool usage inform trade-offs between autonomy, cost, and auditability relevant to copilot design.
Relevance Score: High - it empirically measures detection accuracy and incident resolution/remediation time with an autonomous LLM-agentic AIOps approach, directly matching the thesis focus even though the MTTD/MTTR labels are not used.

Title: TAMO: Fine-Grained Root Cause Analysis via Tool-Assisted LLM Agent With Multi-Modality Observation Data in Cloud-Native Systems
Authors: Xiao Zhang; Qi Wang; Mingyi Li; Yuan Yuan; Mengbai Xiao; Fuzhen Zhuang; Dongxiao Yu
Year & Venue: 2025; IEEE Transactions on Services Computing (TSC), Vol. 18, No. 6, November/December 2025, pp. 4221-4233; DOI 10.1109/TSC.2025.3629066
Core Problem Addressed: Fine-grained root cause analysis (RCA) in cloud-native microservice systems, where existing LLM-based approaches face three challenges: multi-modality input constraint (most support only log or code data, ignoring metrics/traces), context window limitation (LLMs cannot ingest massive real-time metric data), and dynamic dependence graphs (evolving service call chains hinder modeling of fault propagation paths) (Sec. I, p. 4221-4222)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: TAMO: a tool-assisted LLM agent framework with three domain-specific tools and one agent: T1 multi-modality alignment tool (dual-branch collaborative diffusion model with patch-based Transformer backbone, conditioned on Drain-extracted log patterns/TF-IDF keywords and trace KPIs) unifying logs, traces, and metrics into time-aligned representations; T2 root cause localization tool (FFT high-pass filtering + frequency-domain self-attention causal graph + GAT to simulate fault propagation); T3 fault types classification tool (Transformer encoder + GAT + MLP with weighted BCE loss); and an RCA Expert Agent A using GPT-4, which synthesizes T2/T3 outputs plus system context via structured prompts to produce a fault analysis report and repair suggestions for site reliability engineers (human-in-the-loop: outputs assist engineers rather than executing autonomous remediation) (Sec. III, p. 4223-4227, Figs. 2-3)
Methodology: Empirical/controlled experiments on two public benchmark datasets: Dataset A (AIOps Challenge, fault injection into HipsterShop microservice system; 10 services, 4 pods each = 40 pods on 6 nodes; metrics, logs, traces; 15 fault types) and Dataset B (SocialNetwork system, 21 microservices, Chaosblade fault injection, 3 fault types); baselines: Eadro, HolisticRCA, TimesNet, SegRNN, DejaVu, Transformer, LightGBM; metrics: Acc@1/3/5 for localization and micro/macro Precision, Recall, F1 for classification; implementation on NVIDIA RTX 3090, PyTorch 2.4.0, staged training (T1 pre-trained then frozen, then T2, T3, joint fine-tuning 5 epochs); plus ablation study, hyperparameter sensitivity, efficiency analysis, and a real-world case study on HipsterShop (Sec. IV, p. 4227-4230)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified. The paper does not report MTTD, MTTR, alert fatigue, or resolution-time measurements; impact is qualitative only: RCA aims at "minimizing human intervention" and agent outputs help engineers take "reasonable remediation actions, thus enhancing system reliability and response efficiency" (Sec. I, p. 4221; Sec. III-D, p. 4226)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: TAMO outperforms SOTA with average Acc@1 improvement of 4.8% (root cause localization) and MiPr improvement of 10.8% (fault types classification); on dataset An it reaches MiPr 0.8718 and MiF1 0.8831, beating HolisticRCA by 24.99% and 19.85%; MiPr 0.7164 (As) and 0.7182 (Ap) exceed best baselines by 8.09% and 12.69%; efficiency: training 0.81 s/epoch (Dataset B) and 5.7 s (Dataset A), inference 0.17 s/sample (slightly slower than Eadro but meets real-time RCA needs); parameters: T1 9.32M, T2 1.38M, T3 258.32K; case study: 97.96% localization confidence for Currency Service and 82.39% for CheckoutPod0, and the tool-assisted agent produced accurate analysis while a raw-data LLM showed "significant omissions and misjudgments" due to context limitations; ablations show removing T1, the time branch, or FFT degrades performance (Sec. I, p. 4222; Sec. IV, p. 4228-4231, Tables II-IV, Figs. 5-7)
Limitations / Future Work: ⚠ Ambiguous: the paper has no explicit limitations or future work section. Implicit limitations reported in results: performance is highly sensitive to hyperparameter beta ("minor changes causing sharp accuracy drops"); mu at boundary values (0 or 1) causes significant degradation; inference is slightly slower than Eadro; some baselines required dataset partitioning due to entity heterogeneity; datasets are fault-injection benchmarks rather than production incidents (Sec. IV-F, p. 4229-4230, Fig. 4)
Relevance to My Thesis: TAMO is a concrete instance of an agentic LLM copilot for incident response: a GPT-4 expert agent orchestrating specialized perception tools over multi-modal observability data (logs, metrics, traces) to localize root causes, classify fault types, and recommend remediations to SREs. It directly addresses the diagnosis phase that drives MTTD/MTTR, and its tool-decoupling design solves the context-window and modality problems any observability copilot faces. However, it evaluates accuracy metrics (Acc@K, F1) rather than MTTD/MTTR, so for the thesis it serves as architectural and methodological evidence (tool-assisted single-agent design, human-in-the-loop reporting, benchmark datasets HipsterShop/SocialNetwork) rather than direct metric evidence. Its comparison of tool-assisted vs. raw-data LLM output also supports the argument that agentic scaffolding is necessary for reliable incident copilots.
Relevance Score: Medium — an LLM-agent AIOps/RCA framework highly adjacent to the thesis (incident diagnosis copilot with multi-modal observability), but it does not measure MTTD or MTTR directly.

Title: AgentAI: A comprehensive survey on autonomous agents in distributed AI for industry 4.0
Authors: Francesco Piccialli; Diletta Chiaro; Sundas Sarwar; Donato Cerciello; Pian Qi; Valeria Mele
Year & Venue: 2025; Expert Systems With Applications (ESWA), Elsevier, vol. 291, article 128404 (Review article)
Core Problem Addressed: Existing surveys on AgentAI examine it only in "fragmented or application-specific contexts, with limited focus on agent autonomy and architectural frameworks", lacking a comprehensive cross-sectoral perspective; the paper fills this gap with a multi-domain taxonomy analyzing both non-autonomous and fully autonomous AgentAI systems in Industry 4.0 (Sec. 1.2, p. 2; Abstract, p. 1)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Survey (no new system): synthesizes AgentAI architecture as perception, cognition, and action modules (Sec. 3.1, p. 4); core techniques RL/DRL/MARL (QMIX, G2ANet), transformers, and LLMs (GPT-3/4, Llama, Gemini, DeepSeek) plus alternative paradigms (symbolic reasoning, graph-based policies, behaviour trees, probabilistic/Bayesian agents) (Sec. 3.2, pp. 4-6); an AgentAI lifecycle (creation, deployment, migration, integration, shutdown) with human-in-the-loop supervision and interruptibility in high-risk domains (Sec. 3.3, pp. 6-7); and a taxonomy of 66 works across nine Industry 4.0 domains: Transportation, Energy, Healthcare, Networking, Defence, Gaming, Governance, Marketing, E-Learning (Sec. 5, p. 8)
Methodology: SLR following PRISMA guidelines; search of Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ScienceDirect with query TITLE-ABS-KEY ("AgentAI" OR "AgenticAI" OR "Agentic AI"); 255 initial articles (130 Scopus, 64 WoS, 25 ScienceDirect, 36 IEEE Xplore) reduced to 144 after removing non-English and duplicates, then to a final set of 66 experimental articles (reviews/surveys excluded, past decade only); screening artifacts shared via a public GitHub repository (Sec. 2, p. 3)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable — no MTTD, MTTR, alert-fatigue, or incident-resolution metrics are reported in this survey; qualitatively, anomaly detection in robots is said to reduce "waste and downtime" (Sec. 4, p. 8), LLM-based multi-agent smart-city systems shorten "decision-making cycles from days to hours" (Sec. 5.1, p. 9), and Industry 6.0 agents are envisioned to monitor system health and execute recovery actions in self-healing ecosystems (Sec. 6.3, p. 15)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Reports surveyed results: MARL (QMIX, G2ANet) in wastewater treatment achieved "up to a 25 % reduction in aeration energy consumption and a 7 % improvement in effluent quality" (Sec. 5.2, p. 9); LLM-based multi-agent urban systems improve query routing accuracy (94 %-99 %) (Sec. 5.1, p. 9); fine-tuning lets agents execute tasks more efficiently, optimizing computational costs and reducing latency (Sec. 3, p. 4); documented multi-agent failure modes include coordination failures, adversarial conduct, and input spoofing (Sec. 5.7, p. 12); human-in-the-loop control remains essential in high-risk domains for output verification, ethical alignment, and exception handling (Sec. 3.3, p. 6)
Limitations / Future Work: Challenges: agents struggle with evolving goals, changing contexts, and high-modality observations; multi-agent frameworks rest on idealized communication assumptions that break down under latency, noise, and incomplete data; scalability, data scarcity, fragmented data silos, limited interoperability, and poor generalizability of simulation-trained models; tension between autonomy and human oversight (Sec. 6.1-6.2, p. 14). Future work: real-time adaptability, context-aware reasoning, privacy-preserving mechanisms, human-centric Industry 5.0 collaboration, and an Industry 6.0 blueprint of decentralized multi-agent coordination, intention inference, and self-managing, self-healing infrastructure (Sec. 6.2-6.3, pp. 14-15)
Relevance to My Thesis: This survey supplies conceptual scaffolding for the thesis rather than incident-response evidence. Its perception-cognition-action component model, comparison of agent paradigms, and lifecycle stages (including human-in-the-loop supervision and interruptibility) can ground the architectural framing of an Agentic AI copilot for incident response. The Industry 6.0 vision of agents that monitor system health, execute recovery actions, and rebalance workloads without centralized oversight directly parallels self-healing AIOps goals behind MTTD/MTTR reduction. Its catalogued multi-agent failure modes (coordination failures, input spoofing) and challenges (latency, noisy data, oversight balance) inform threat and limitation sections. However, it offers no incident-management metrics or IT-operations case studies, so it serves as background/taxonomy support only.
Relevance Score: Medium — a comprehensive Agentic AI / multi-agent taxonomy, architecture, and human-in-the-loop lifecycle reference directly supporting the thesis' conceptual foundations, but it targets Industry 4.0 domains and reports no MTTD/MTTR or AIOps/incident-response results.

Title: Artificial intelligence driven multi agent framework for adaptive cyber attack simulation and automated incident response in cyber range environments
Authors: Alka Agrawal; Mohd Nadeem; Ahmed Al Nuaim; Abdullah Al Nuaim
Year & Venue: 2026; Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio journal), vol. 16, article 11673; DOI 10.1038/s41598-026-45937-9; received 9 January 2026, accepted 23 March 2026
Core Problem Addressed: Current cyber range platforms rely on static or rule-based simulation models that cannot represent dynamic, multi-stage, adaptive attack strategies of modern adversaries and lack automated incident response mechanisms; existing AI/MAS studies are not integrated with realistic cyber ranges or validated with real datasets (Sec. Introduction, p. 1; Sec. Problem formulation, p. 5)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: An AI-driven Multi-Agent System (MAS) embedded in the CyDER 2.0 cyber range: attacker agents formulated as an MDP and trained with reinforcement learning (Deep Q-Networks and Policy Gradient) to execute adaptive multi-stage attacks (scan, exploit, privilege escalation, evade); defender agents use a Random Forest + Autoencoder ensemble for anomaly detection plus rule-based automated incident response actions modeled on NIST SP 800-61 (isolate hosts, block IPs, terminate sessions, adjust configurations); agents communicate asynchronously via ZeroMQ with JSON messages and FIPA-compliant ACL, are containerized with Docker, and generate alerts for human operators to continue analysis (human-in-the-loop notification only) (Secs. Model development and Multi-agent system architecture, pp. 8-12; Sec. Model implementation, pp. 12-14; Results, p. 17)
Methodology: Prototype development with simulation-based experimental evaluation: iterative design-implement-evaluate methodology; CICIDS2017 (~80 GB raw) and UNSW-NB15 datasets preprocessed to ~85 features, SMOTE-balanced ~50,000 samples, stratified 80%/20% split (40k train/10k test); three network topologies (Small 50, Medium 120, Large 200 hosts) with 2 attacker and 3 defender agents each; three attack scenarios (A single-stage, B multi-stage, C mixed simultaneous); baselines = static scripted cyber range and rule-based MAS; 10-fold cross-validation, hold-out testing, stress testing, user acceptance testing by cybersecurity experts, paired t-tests and ANOVA; problem statement validated by a survey of 25 cybersecurity experts (5-point Likert, all means > 4.1, p < 0.001) (Sec. Research methodology, pp. 7-8; Sec. Problem formulation, pp. 5-6; Sec. Experimental setup, p. 14; Table 4, p. 12)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: MTTD and MTTR are not named; the analogous metric is average response latency (time between attack detection and start of response): AI-driven MAS 4.2 s (Small), 5.6 s (Medium), 6.1 s (Large) vs. rule-based MAS 6.5-9.5 s and static cyber range 12.1-18.4 s (Table 10, p. 16); "The time taken for responses is also reduced by 35%" vs. non-adaptive baselines (Sec. Results, p. 17); detection F1-scores 94.5%/89.9%/87.9% vs. rule-based 80.1%/75.5%/71.8% and static 67.8%/59.2%/56.1% (Table 9, p. 15); F1-score reported as 25% higher than the non-adaptive version (Sec. Results, p. 17); latency stays below the cited sub-10-second operational threshold for timely mitigation (Sec. Average response latency, p. 16); alert fatigue Not specified
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Agent-to-environment action execution latency avg 85 ms +/- 15 ms with 99.8% message delivery reliability (Table 7, p. 14); per-agent resource cost: attacker 35% +/- 5 CPU / 140 +/- 15 MB RAM, defender 30% +/- 4 CPU / 130 +/- 12 MB RAM, inter-agent communication used < 5% of network resources (Table 12 and Observations, pp. 16-17); attack complexity scores 5/12/15 vs. rule-based 3/7/9 and static 2/4/5 across network sizes (Table 11, p. 16); attacker RL converged by ~episode 4200 of 5000 with 84.5% final attack success rate (Table 5, p. 13; Observations, p. 17); validation summary reports > 99.5% uptime, graceful fault handling, linear resource use in scaling tests (Table 13, p. 17); comparative analysis: 91% accuracy, 5.3 s latency, scales to 25+ agents vs. prior models at 65-78% accuracy and < 5 agents (Table 14, pp. 17-18)
Limitations / Future Work: Authors state that running the AI-driven MAS on resource-constrained distributed edge devices will be challenging from computation and storage perspectives; future work includes model compression techniques, lightweight inference models, and hybrid edge-cloud deployment architectures (Sec. Conclusion, p. 18); the incident response module itself remains a predefined rule-based action library rather than a learned policy (Sec. Results, p. 17); reported CPU/memory figures assume a server-class cyber range environment (Sec. Conclusion, p. 18)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper offers a validated multi-agent architecture in which autonomous detection agents trigger automated incident response, directly analogous to the agentic copilot loop the thesis targets: its response-latency metric (4.2-6.1 s vs. 12.1-18.4 s static) is a concrete proxy for MTTR reduction, and its detection F1 gains map to MTTD improvement. Its measured orchestration costs (85 ms agent latency, 99.8% message reliability, per-agent CPU/RAM) provide reusable benchmarks for evaluating multi-agent overhead in incident response pipelines. The human-in-the-loop element (alerting operators for further analysis after automated containment) mirrors the copilot posture of the thesis. However, the context is cybersecurity training in a cyber range, uses RL/ML rather than LLM-based agents, and never frames results in MTTD/MTTR or SRE/AIOps terms, so its evidence transfers only by analogy to production incident management.
Relevance Score: Medium - it quantitatively demonstrates that an AI-driven multi-agent system reduces incident response time (35% reduction; 4.2-6.1 s vs. up to 18.4 s baselines) and improves detection, but in a cybersecurity cyber range training context without LLM copilots and without explicit MTTD/MTTR metrics, making it adjacent rather than direct evidence for the thesis.

Title: Surveying Root Cause Analysis Techniques: A Comprehensive Review of Aspects for Multi-Service Applications
Authors: Zhijing Li; Jianbo Yu; Zhijun Huang; Yusheng Huang
Year & Venue: 2026 (accepted 8 November 2025; published 13 November 2025); IEEE Transactions on Services Computing (TSC), Vol. 19, No. 1, January/February 2026
Core Problem Addressed: Root Cause Analysis (RCA) techniques remain "highly fragmented, often developed for isolated domains and lacking integration across multi-service environments"; complex interdependencies among monitoring components in distributed, microservice, and cloud-based systems make identifying the root cause of failures a crucial but difficult operation and maintenance task (Sec. I, p. 808-809)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Not a proposed system but a survey: it organizes RCA methods along two orthogonal axes - application scenarios (cloud services, microservices, industrial systems) and input-data types (logs, traces, metrics, reports) - and synthesizes algorithmic families, hybrid/LLM approaches, datasets, tools, and evaluation metrics (Abstract; Sec. I, p. 808-809); regarding agentic AI, it reviews LLM-based RCA: fine-tuned GPT-3.x inferring root causes and fixes from 40K+ Microsoft incident summaries [64], a ReAct-based LLM agent retrieving logs, metrics, and incident tickets for out-of-distribution RCA [65], and the OpenRCA benchmark for LLM agents [66] (Sec. VII, p. 815)
Methodology: Systematic literature review following Kitchenham et al. guidelines; structured keyword search across five databases (Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, DBLP, Scopus); 96 keyword-venue combination queries via an automated crawler; studies published 2017-2025; 845 papers collected, 97 peer-reviewed studies selected after inclusion/exclusion criteria; graph-based analysis used to map research connections (Sec. II, p. 809-810)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified as MTTD/MTTR values; only a qualitative claim that log analysis "can be found quickly, leading to a faster time to identify and fix problems" (Sec. III.B, p. 811); the survey's reviewed evaluation metrics are Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-Score, Top@N (e.g., AC@k, PR@k, HR@k), MRR, runtime, FP/FN, and clustering metrics - not detection/recovery time metrics (Sec. X, p. 820-822)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Reports third-party results: fine-tuned LLMs "surpass encoder-decoder baselines in generating effective explanations and mitigation plans" on 40K+ Microsoft incidents [64]; a ReAct-based LLM agent matches strong baselines with higher factual accuracy, while post-mortem comments offer no added benefit [65]; on the OpenRCA benchmark (335 failures, 68 GB telemetry) "even the best LLM agent solves only 11.3% of cases" [66]; LLM-based methods are "constrained by limited context, susceptibility to hallucinations, and low real-world success rates" (Sec. VII, p. 815; Sec. XII, p. 822)

XIII, p. 823); open issues: algorithmic limitations (correlation/heuristic methods fail to capture true causality; lack of interpretability), scarcity of large-scale, realistic, multi-modal RCA datasets, and poor cross-domain generalization; future work: improved LLM contextual understanding and reduced hallucinations, multimodal telemetry fusion (logs, traces, metrics, topology), and explainable real-time RCA tools with causal reasoning and streaming inference (Sec. XII, p. 822-823)
Relevance to My Thesis: This survey maps the RCA landscape that an Agentic AI incident-response copilot must operate in, organizing techniques by telemetry input (logs, traces, metrics, reports) and scenario (cloud, microservices) - directly matching the observability data a copilot would consume to reduce MTTD/MTTR. Its Section VII on hybrid and LLM-based RCA, especially the ReAct agent study and the OpenRCA finding that the best LLM agent solves only 11.3% of cases, provides sobering baseline evidence for the feasibility claims of my thesis. Relevance Score: Medium - it is an adjacent AIOps/RCA survey covering LLM-agent approaches and observability data highly relevant to an incident-response copilot, but it does not measure MTTD/MTTR with an agentic approach.

Title: Leveraging multi-agent framework for root cause analysis
Authors: Feng Fu; Hong Ding; Yong Qin; Jian Yu; Dechao Xu
Year & Venue: 2026 (journal issue; published online 6 November 2025); Complex & Intelligent Systems, vol. 12, article 4, Springer; DOI 10.1007/s40747-025-02096-0
Core Problem Addressed: Automated root cause analysis (RCA) in complex integrated systems (cloud-native platforms, distributed power metering infrastructures) faces three challenges: complex mapping between anomalies and runtime data, semantic gap between unstructured logs and structured metrics, and combinatorial explosion of causal relationships; additionally, LLM hallucinations and context-switching failures in single-agent multi-step RCA reasoning lead to incorrect root cause identification (Abstract, p. 1; Introduction, pp. 1-2)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: MA-RCA, a collaborative multi-agent framework with four specialized agents: RCA Agent (central orchestrator: semantic parsing of anomaly reports with strict extraction of device type, symptom, device ID, timeframe; agent scheduling; probabilistic root cause synthesis); Retrieval Agent (RAG over a historical anomaly case repository using hybrid keyword+semantic retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, and LLM-based root cause inversion with reverse indices and symptom generalization); Validation Agent (decomposes hypotheses into quantifiable indicators, LSH-based task deduplication, priority-aware toolchain execution via APIs such as Prometheus and Modbus/TCP, TTL cache pool, BERT-embedding semantic similarity confidence scoring); Report Agent (adaptive-template diagnostic reports, PDF export, IEC/NERC compliance); human-in-the-loop: SREs submit natural-language alerts and are re-queried when required parameters are missing; base LLMs tested include QwenMax (best), DeepSeek, LLAMA3.3-70B, Qwen-QwQ (Method, Figs. 1-2, Algorithms 1-2, pp. 3-7; Table 5, p. 10)
Methodology: Prototype framework with controlled experimental evaluation on two datasets: (1) Nezha benchmark (open-source, multi-modal observability from OnlineBoutique with 56 fault instances (42 resource, 14 code) and TrainTicket with 45 instances (21 resource, 24 code); stratified 50%/50% split into historical cases vs. evaluation; pre-processed telemetry, not live instrumentation); (2) a proprietary real-world Power monitoring dataset (ICT infrastructure and electrical system faults, 231 instances per Table 2); baselines: CoT, RAG, RCACOPILOT, RCAgent, mABC; metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1; plus ablation study (4 variants), base-LLM comparison, retrieval-count sensitivity study, and a real-world system illustration deploying MA-RCA as a "Diagnosis Agent" plugin in a power metering system (Evaluation, Tables 1-6, pp. 7-11; System illustration, Figs. 3-4, pp. 11-12)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified — no MTTD, MTTR, alert-fatigue, or resolution-time measurements are reported; qualitative statements only: "the Report Agent reduces manual report generation time" (Report Agent, p. 7), and the authors acknowledge data collection/validation "introduce additional latency compared to direct inference methods" in time-sensitive scenarios (Conclusions, p. 12)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: MA-RCA achieves Nezha Acc = 0.958, F1 = 0.952 (best baseline RCACOPILOT F1 = 0.748) and Power monitoring Acc = 0.843, F1 = 0.828 (best baseline F1 = 0.651) (Table 3, p. 9); ablations: w/o multi-agent F1 drops to 0.716 (Nezha) / 0.680 (Power); w/o Retrieval Agent to 0.295 / 0.144; w/o semantic retrieval to 0.874 / 0.663; w/o Validation Agent to 0.681 / 0.543 (Table 4, p. 10); mABC-style full-workflow multi-agent voting is said to amplify computational overhead (p. 8); performance robust across base LLMs (F1 0.809-0.828, Table 5, p. 10); retrieval count is non-monotonic with optimum at 5 cases (Acc 0.798 at 1 case, 0.843 at 5, 0.812 at 20; Table 6, p. 11)
Limitations / Future Work: (1) "its effectiveness depends heavily on the quality and comprehensiveness of the historical case repository"; sparse or outdated data may constrain the Retrieval Agent; (2) data collection and validation introduce additional latency vs. direct inference, affecting usability in highly time-sensitive scenarios; future work: adaptive retrieval mechanisms to dynamically set the number/relevance of retrieved cases beyond static top-k, and speculative execution/pre-fetching strategies for the agent team to parallelize data collection (Conclusions, p. 12)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper provides a directly reusable multi-agent architecture (orchestrator, retrieval, validation, reporting agents) for the diagnosis phase of incident response, which is the core activity an agentic copilot must automate to reduce MTTR. Its two anti-hallucination mechanisms — RAG grounding in historical incident cases and tool-based hypothesis validation against runtime telemetry — are strong design patterns for a trustworthy SRE copilot, and the ablations quantify how much each agent contributes. The human-in-the-loop input parsing (SRE submits a natural-language alert, agent re-queries for missing fields) matches the copilot interaction model of my thesis. However, evaluation is limited to RCA classification accuracy/F1, so the thesis would need to add MTTD/MTTR instrumentation on top of such a framework; the acknowledged validation latency is a relevant trade-off to measure.
Relevance Score: Medium — an LLM-based multi-agent framework applied directly to incident root cause analysis (AIOps-adjacent) with strong quantitative results, but it evaluates classification accuracy/F1 and reports no MTTD/MTTR or resolution-time metrics.

Title: A Multi-Agent System for Cybersecurity Threat Detection and Correlation Using Large Language Models
Authors: Yasser Hmimou; Mohamed Tabaa; Azeddine Khiat; Zineb Hidila
Year & Venue: 2025; IEEE Access, vol. 13 (published 25 August 2025; DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2025.3602681)
Core Problem Addressed: Traditional rule-based IDS and signature-based tools detect known threats but lack contextual understanding and semantic interpretation, creating "a critical gap in detecting coordinated or subtle attack patterns that span multiple systems and domains" (e.g., spear-phishing, APTs, multi-stage attacks); siloed detection cannot correlate indicators across email, logs, and IP communications (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. I, p. 2)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Modular, workflow-driven multi-agent architecture with four layers: a task dispatcher agent (input validation, task classification, asynchronous routing), three specialized agents — email verification (FAISS vector similarity, RegEx, tldextract, dns.resolver + RAG), log analyzer (ELK stack normalization, Suricata signatures + LLM contextual interpretation, memory module), IP range analyzer (Nmap, NVD/CVE lookup + LLM risk explanation) — and a central contextual recommendation system that normalizes agent outputs, applies RegEx entity matching and temporal correlation, assigns correlation confidence, and synthesizes narrative threat reports; all agents use LLaMA 3.3-70B via the Groq API with chain-of-thought prompting and selective RAG; LLMs act as deterministic, prompt-driven semantic processors "not as autonomous decision makers", keeping human analysts in oversight (Sec. IV-C, pp. 9-10; Sec. V-A/B, pp. 11-13)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: MTTD and MTTR are not measured by name (Not specified as formal metrics); adjacent incident-handling results: analyst triage time "decreased by 38.5% on average due to clear, contextual explanations"; false positive alerts reduced by 41.3% versus a traditional SIEM baseline (alert-fatigue proxy); analyst confidence averaged 4.6 on a 5-point scale; outputs are said to accelerate "informed decision-making and incident response" (Sec. V-B, pp. 12-13; Fig. 10, p. 14; Sec. III-E, p. 8)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Full pipeline: 93.6% detection accuracy, 87.0% multi-agent correlation accuracy, F1 score 0.94, outperforming 12 compared LLM/multi-agent systems; agent-level classification accuracy 91.8%-94.1%; over 90% of LLM-generated explanations judged technically valid and useful (IP agent highest explanation success at 93.2%; log analyzer lower FPR performance); in most of the 60 tasks two or more agents jointly contributed to the final decision; Groq inference API "significantly reduces latency and computational overhead compared to local deployments"; constraining LLMs to deterministic workflows is credited with interpretability, reproducibility, and reduced inter-module inconsistency (Sec. V-B, pp. 12-14; Tables 5-7; Fig. 12, p. 15; Sec. III-B, p. 5)
Limitations / Future Work: Limitations: reliance on third-party tools/APIs (Nmap, Groq) can "cause latency issues" and become single points of failure; LLM explanation generation adds computational cost and potential unpredictability across prompt construction or model updates; legacy datasets (SpamAssassin, CIC-IDS 2017) limit evaluation against emerging threats. Future work: multimodal inputs (attachments, links, visual payloads), real-time continuous log-stream analysis, federated deployment for distributed/privacy-constrained infrastructure, lighter LLM variants for edge/low-bandwidth deployment, asynchronous execution and resilience strategies (Sec. VI, p. 15)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper is a strong architectural analogue for an Agentic AI copilot in incident response: specialized LLM-enhanced agents plus a central correlation layer mirror the detect-correlate-explain loop that drives MTTD/MTTR. Its quantified 38.5% analyst triage-time reduction and 41.3% false-positive reduction versus a SIEM baseline are directly reusable evidence that agentic correlation reduces alert fatigue and resolution effort, even though MTTD/MTTR are not measured explicitly. The deliberate design choice of workflow-constrained (non-autonomous) LLMs with chain-of-thought, RAG, and full prompt/output audit trails offers a concrete human-in-the-loop pattern for a copilot the thesis can adopt. Its two-stage evaluation protocol (per-agent validation plus blind analyst rating of 60 end-to-end tasks) is a transferable methodology for measuring copilot impact on incident metrics.
Relevance Score: Medium — adjacent security-operations domain with an LLM multi-agent system that quantifies triage-time (38.5%) and false-positive (41.3%) reductions, but does not directly measure MTTD or MTTR.

Title: AIOps for log anomaly detection in the era of LLMs: A systematic literature review
Authors: Miguel De la Cruz Cabello; Tiago Prince Sales; Marcos R. Machado
Year & Venue: 2025; Intelligent Systems with Applications (Elsevier), vol. 28, art. 200608; received 13 July 2025, available online 19 November 2025
Core Problem Addressed: Modern IT systems generate large volumes of log data that challenge timely and effective anomaly detection; traditional methods "often require intensive feature engineering and struggle to adapt to dynamic operational environments", limiting scalability, contextual awareness, and adaptability to new anomaly types (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 1, p. 2)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: SLR synthesizing how AIOps benefits from LLMs for log anomaly detection, showing prompt engineering and RAG boost accuracy and interpretability without extensive fine-tuning; contributes a taxonomy of LLM/RAG-based methods along three dimensions (Model Architecture; Knowledge Augmentation Strategy; Inference Objective) and a CRISP-ML-mapped framework with three stages (project definition; vector-database construction; LLM+RAG anomaly detection with output evaluation); reviewed agentic examples include ChatCNC's three LLM agents (Question Identifier, Data Retriever, Response Generator) and Loevenich et al.'s MARL+LLM+rule-based autonomous cyber defense agents; LLMs positioned "as an external tool to help IT operators, system administrators, and maintainers" (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 4.2-4.4, pp. 12-14; Sec. 5, p. 14)
Methodology: Systematic Literature Review: 4 knowledge questions; Scopus as primary database plus arXiv via backward/forward snowballing (Wohlin, 2014); 3 search queries combining AIOps, anomaly/incident detection, LLMs, RAG, military keywords; inclusion/exclusion criteria (conference/journal papers, computer science/engineering, English, published 2021 onwards for initial search, free version available); 33 articles total (23 from Scopus queries); quality assessed via titles/abstracts; data extracted into appendix table; VOSviewer keyword network analysis (Sec. 2, p. 3; Fig. 1-2, pp. 3-4; Sec. 3.3, p. 4)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: No MTTD/MTTR measurements; MTTD, MTTR, and alert fatigue are not used as evaluation metrics in any reviewed study — dominant metrics are F1-score, precision, recall, AUROC (Sec. 4.2, p. 10; Sec. 5, p. 14; Table A1). Qualitative only: AIOps enables "more streamlined operations and faster incident resolution", rapid detection/diagnosis of bottlenecks, and reduced downtime and operational costs (Sec. 4.1, p. 7); reviewed quantitative detection results include LogLLM F1-scores on average 6.6% better than existing methods and RAPID overall F1-score of 0.97 (Sec. 4.2, p. 9); real-time gap noted: with a 10 s failure-perception window the model must infer within 1 s, and "no LLM-based work has adequately tackled this problem" (Sec. 4.4, p. 13)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: LLM-based approaches outperform traditional methods on F1-score/precision/recall and improve interpretability; RAG mitigates hallucinations, outdated knowledge, and domain drift by injecting external context, outperforming fine-tuning in Ovadia et al.'s experiments (Sec. 4.2-4.3, pp. 9-10). Trade-offs reported: full-sized LLMs incur higher memory/compute, inference latency, GPU/API costs; RAG adds vector-database and embedding costs plus pipeline complexity (retrieval, prompt engineering, vector DB maintenance), privacy risks with third-party models, and drift/hallucination monitoring needs (Sec. 4.2, p. 10; Sec. 4.3, p. 12). Multi-agent evidence is peripheral: ChatCNC three-agent RAG system evaluated by human raters (1-5 scale) and MARL+LLM blue agents defending simulated NATO-inspired military networks (Sec. 4.3, p. 11; Sec. 4.4, p. 12)
Limitations / Future Work: Scopus/arXiv coverage "not entirely exhaustive", potentially introducing selection bias (footnote 11, Sec. 2, p. 3); benchmark datasets (HDFS, BGL, Thunderbird, Liberty) are narrow, with post-hoc human labels that can introduce bias, limiting generalizability (Sec. 4.3, pp. 11-12); F1/precision/recall are sensitive to class imbalance and may not reflect domain priorities — future work should add MCC, AUC-PR, and domain-specific cost functions (Sec. 4.2, p. 10); most studies operate offline, limiting timeliness (Sec. 4.4, p. 13); future directions: real-time anomaly detection pipelines, RAG tailored to log datasets (storing log templates in vector databases), and military-domain log analytics where research remains scarce (Sec. 4.4, pp. 13-14)
Relevance to My Thesis: This SLR maps the AIOps pipeline (preprocessing, failure perception, root cause analysis, auto-remediation) in which an Agentic AI copilot for incident response would operate, and anomaly detection is the stage that directly conditions MTTD. Its evidence that LLM+RAG approaches outperform traditional detection methods supports the design choice of an LLM-based copilot grounded in operational context via retrieval. Critically, it confirms a gap my thesis targets: none of the 33 reviewed studies evaluates MTTD/MTTR or operator-facing incident metrics, relying instead on F1/precision/recall, and no LLM-based work handles the real-time (sub-second inference) constraint of live incident detection. The cost/latency/hallucination trade-off analysis and the proposed CRISP-ML framework offer reusable design and evaluation considerations for building and validating a copilot prototype.
Relevance Score: Medium — directly adjacent (AIOps, LLM-based log anomaly detection, RAG for IT operations) but does not measure MTTD/MTTR and covers agentic/multi-agent systems only peripherally.

Title: Reliability of LLM Inference Engines from a Static Perspective: Root Cause Analysis and Repair Suggestion via Natural Language Reports
Authors: Hongwei Li; Yongjun Wang
Year & Venue: 2026; Big Data and Cognitive Computing (BDCC), MDPI; vol. 10, article 60; published 13 February 2026
Core Problem Addressed: Defects in LLM inference engines (e.g., vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) are numerous, hard to localize, and costly to fix, yet existing reliability/defect-analysis techniques assume executable code, runtime environments, or dynamic traces that are impractical for these hardware-dependent systems; there is also no publicly available annotated dataset of real-world inference-engine defects (Sec. 1, pp. 1-2)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: A static, execution-free, three-stage pipeline over GitHub issue reports: (1) root cause classification via TF-IDF (unigrams+bigrams) + class-weighted multinomial logistic regression into 4 semantic categories (model_execution, runtime_state, resource_concurrency, io_semantic); (2) coarse-grained module localization via TF-IDF cosine similarity between issue text and module textual profiles; (3) repair suggestion generation by an off-the-shelf LLM (ChatGPT/GPT-5.2 and Qwen3-235B-A22B, no fine-tuning) guided by structured prompts embedding predicted root cause, module, and predefined root cause-repair patterns. The LLM is used "solely as a conditional text generator"; diagnosis is done by deterministic/statistical components; no agentic or multi-agent orchestration; human developers consume the suggestions (Sec. 3, pp. 4-9; Sec. 4, pp. 9-10)
Methodology: Empirical study with prototype evaluation on real-world data: manually annotated dataset of closed bug-labeled GitHub issues (data snapshot January 2026) - 176 vLLM issues + 100 TensorRT-LLM issues; stratified 5-fold cross-validation (80/20) for classification; cross-engine transfer test (train on vLLM, test on TensorRT-LLM); scalability timing experiments; human evaluation of 50 randomly sampled issues by 5 researchers on 5-point Likert scales (Correctness, Usefulness, Clarity) with Fleiss' kappa inter-rater reliability; environment: Ubuntu 22.04, Intel Xeon Gold 6430, 256 GB RAM, Python 3.10, scikit-learn, no GPU needed (Sec. 5.1-5.5, pp. 11-14)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable - no MTTD, MTTR, alert-fatigue, or incident-resolution-time metrics are measured. Qualitative only: module localization puts the correct module in the top two predictions in over 84% of cases, so developers "only need to focus on inspecting a subset of candidate modules rather than searching the entire codebase", reducing the debugging search space (Sec. 5.3, pp. 12-13)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: No agentic/multi-agent system is evaluated; results concern a single-LLM-assisted static pipeline: root cause classification accuracy 68.8%, Macro-F1 0.421 (+18.8 percentage points over Linear SVM and Random Forest, both 0.500); TF-IDF+LSA variant 0.682/0.416; module localization Top-1 0.705, Top-2 0.841 vs. 0.182/0.304 most-frequent baseline; cross-engine (vLLM to TensorRT-LLM) accuracy 64.0%, Macro-F1 0.405; localization time tens of milliseconds for 140 issues with near-linear scaling; human evaluation (ChatGPT-5.2): Correctness 3.7, Usefulness 3.6, Clarity 4.3; Qwen3-235B-A22B: 3.5/3.4/4.1 (Fleiss' kappa 0.48/0.44/0.61), indicating the framework is "largely model-agnostic"; authors note a cascading failure mode: upstream misclassification yields generic or partially relevant repair suggestions (Sec. 5.2-5.5, pp. 11-15)
Limitations / Future Work: Limitations: effectiveness constrained by completeness/clarity of issue texts (vague reports yield inaccurate predictions); localization is only coarse module-level, still requiring manual investigation; limited and imbalanced dataset (rare classes like runtime_state remain challenging); classification performance "remains modest"; human evaluation covers few issues and evaluators. Future work: incorporate commits, code diffs, stack traces, dependency relations; extend localization to function/code-block level; expand dataset to more engines and defect categories; move toward fully automated localization and repair (Sec. 5.5, p. 15; Sec. 6, pp. 15-16; Sec. 7, p. 16)
Relevance to My Thesis: The paper's three-stage pipeline (root cause classification, fault localization, LLM-generated remediation guidance) is structurally analogous to the diagnose-localize-remediate loop an Agentic AI incident-response copilot must perform, and its evidence that constrained, structured prompts grounded in deterministic upstream analysis reduce LLM hallucination is directly reusable for copilot design. Its finding that repair-suggestion quality cascades from upstream classification accuracy warns about error propagation in multi-stage agent pipelines relevant to MTTR reduction. However, it targets offline software bug triage for LLM inference engines, not production incident response, and reports no MTTD/MTTR or operational metrics, so it serves mainly as methodological inspiration and as evidence for the reliability challenges of the LLM serving infrastructure that copilots themselves depend on.
Relevance Score: Low - the paper contains no agentic/multi-agent architecture and no MTTD/MTTR or incident-management measurements; it is tangential (LLM-assisted software defect root cause analysis and repair suggestion for inference engines), offering only conceptual analogies to incident-response copilots.

Title: GALR: Graph-Based Root Cause Localization and LLM-Assisted Recovery for Microservice Systems
Authors: Wenya Zhang; Zhi Yang; Fang Peng; Le Zhang; Yiting Chen; Ruibo Chen
Year & Venue: 2026; Electronics (MDPI journal), vol. 15, article 243; received 14 November 2025, published 5 January 2026
Core Problem Addressed: Fast and accurate root cause localization and recovery in large-scale, complex microservice systems, where multimodal runtime signals (metrics, logs, traces) intertwined with deep dynamic service dependencies lead to noisy alerts, ambiguous fault propagation paths, and brittle manually curated recovery playbooks; additionally, diagnosis and recovery are often treated as separate stages, logs are reduced to coarse templates, and LLM outputs lack structural grounding and verification (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 1, p. 2)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: GALR, a graph- and LLM-based framework: (1) multimodal service call graph fusing time-series metrics, structured logs, and trace-derived topology; (2) GAT-based root cause localization with temporal decay edge attention; (3) LLM-based node enhancement that infers a probability triplet [anomaly, normal, uncertainty] from log contexts and injects it into node representations and a semantic attention bias term; (4) a retrieval-augmented LLM recovery agent that retrieves similar historical cases from a 500-case library (BGE-M3 embeddings, cosine similarity) and generates structured recovery plans (action steps, verification metrics, rollback strategies), verified via action-overlap consistency checking against expert-standard playbooks; DeepSeek V3 is the LLM used; human-in-the-loop: unsafe plans "should be rejected or escalated for manual confirmation" (Sec. 3, pp. 5-11; Sec. 4.3, p. 13; Sec. 5, p. 16)
Methodology: Controlled experiments with fault injection on three microservice datasets: Customer Service (23,183 traces, 67 services, 24 injected faults), Power Grid Resource (19,872 traces, 89 services, 32 faults), and SockShop (8,981 traces, 15 services, 30 faults) deployed on Kubernetes with Chaos-Mesh fault injection, Locust load generation, Prometheus metrics, and Fluent Bit logs; six fault types (network delay, network loss, CPU stress, memory stress, pod failure, pod kill), single-node single-fault setting, 6:4 train/test split; GAT with two GATConv layers, 4-head attention, AdamW (lr 0.001, batch 32, 30 epochs), weighted BCEWithLogitsLoss; baselines: GCN, GraphSAGE, DiagFusion, MicroRank, MicorEGRCL, PDiagnose; metrics: Top-1/3/10 accuracy, MRR, and recovery strategy accuracy; results averaged over two runs (Sec. 4.1-4.3, pp. 11-13; Sec. 5, p. 16)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: MTTD and MTTR are not directly measured; proxies are reported: root cause localization Top-1 accuracy of 0.842 (Customer Service), 0.883 (Power Grid Resource), 0.931 (SockShop), and average MRR of 0.931 vs. ~0.902 for the strongest baseline (PDiagnose), "a relative improvement of approximately 3.2%"; Top-1 accuracy is stated to reflect "single-step troubleshooting efficiency"; recovery strategy accuracy: LLM + RAG (GALR) 79.2% (SockShop), 75.8% (Power Grid Resource), 70.1% (Customer Service) vs. zero-shot 62.5%/55.1%/48.9% and few-shot 68.9%/61.5%/54.3% (Tables 3-4, pp. 14-15)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: The retrieval-augmented LLM agent substantially outperforms pure zero-shot and few-shot LLM reasoning for recovery generation, showing that grounding in retrieved historical cases improves specificity and feasibility; ablations show removing edge attention, using average-weighted aggregation, or random aggregation consistently degrades MRR (e.g., Customer Service MRR 0.923 full vs. 0.835/0.812/0.781); identified failure modes: LLMs "may still produce incomplete or hallucinated strategies under distribution shifts"; scalability concern that LLM-side annotation/retrieval latency "may hinder near-real-time incident response"; design separates generation from execution with a restricted action space (restart, rollback, migration, scaling) (Sec. 4.4-4.5, pp. 15-16; Table 5, p. 15; Sec. 5, p. 16)
Limitations / Future Work: Limitations: fault injection "does not fully cover the diversity and long-tail characteristics of production incidents"; window-level labels anchored at injection time may miss delayed or cascading effects; recovery plans evaluated offline via action-overlap without live execution, so accuracy reflects action validity not operational success; results averaged over only two runs with no statistical significance testing; scalability/latency bottlenecks for LLM annotation in large graphs; effectiveness depends on multimodal alignment quality and stable logging practices. Future work: (i) selective/incremental LLM annotation with caching and refresh policies, (ii) stricter safety guardrails with constrained action spaces and parameter-level validation, (iii) controlled online verification and better recovery-effectiveness benchmarks (Sec. 5, p. 16; Sec. 6, p. 17)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper directly instantiates the copilot pattern targeted by the thesis: an LLM agent that closes the loop from anomaly perception to root cause localization and recovery planning, the exact activities that drive MTTD and MTTR. Its retrieval-augmented recovery agent with consistency checking against expert playbooks and human escalation of unsafe plans offers a concrete, safety-aware human-in-the-loop design that can be cited as an architectural reference. The Top-1/MRR and recovery-accuracy results provide quantitative evidence that LLM semantic priors improve localization and that RAG grounding beats zero-shot LLM operation, supporting the thesis argument for grounded agentic copilots. However, its lack of direct MTTD/MTTR measurement and offline-only recovery evaluation exemplify the metrics gap the thesis aims to address.
Relevance Score: Medium — strongly adjacent AIOps/LLM-agent work on root cause localization and automated recovery in microservices, but it does not measure MTTD/MTTR directly, reporting Top-k/MRR and action-overlap accuracy instead

Title: A Review of Agentic AI in Cybersecurity: Cognitive Autonomy, Ethical Governance, and Quantum-Resilient Defense [version 1; peer review: 2 approved]

Year & Venue: 2025 (first published 01 Sep 2025); F1000Research, 14:843; DOI 10.12688/f1000research.169337.1
Core Problem Addressed: Conventional cyber defense models relying on static rules, perimeter protections, and human-centric incident response are inadequate against sophisticated threats (APTs, polymorphic malware, adversarial ML), suffering "detection latency, limited adaptability" and inability to counter stealthy long-term intrusions; quantum computing further threatens cryptographic foundations (Sec. 1.2, p. 3; Sec. 1.4.1, pp. 3-4)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Not a system proposal but a synthesis of Agentic AI (autonomous, adaptable, goal-directed agents) for cyber defense across three pillars: cognitive autonomy, ethical governance, quantum-resilient defense. Methodology: Narrative review (explicitly not systematic) of literature 2005-2025 (eligibility window 2010-2025); databases IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, ACM Digital Library plus grey literature (reports, policy briefs); Boolean search with iterative refinement, reference chaining, and selective use of generative AI tools for thematic clustering; five-stage flow (Identify, Screen, Select, Classify, Synthesize) guided by four research questions RQ1-RQ4; number of included studies Not specified (Sec. 2.1-2.6, pp. 7-9)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified quantitatively - no MTTD, MTTR, alert-fatigue, or resolution-time measurements are reported.
