General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Case study: a deployed DRL-agent system with LLM-based analyst interfaces dynamically selected monitoring/deception/remediation strategies, "outperforming baseline static defenses in adversarial testing environments" against simulated red-team attacks (RQ1 case study, p. 14). Quantum-safe pilot: hybrid Kyber/McEliece PQC with AI-driven key management achieved "sub-4ms encryption latency" and zero vulnerability to Shor's algorithm (RQ3 case study, p. 17). Barriers: high cost, legacy integration complexity, skills shortage, ethical concerns; enablers: A2A/MCP protocols, multi-stakeholder collaboration, modular XAI architectures (RQ4, p. 17; Table 5). Bibliometrics: field peaked 2023 with more than 1,200 articles and over 30,000 citations (Sec. 3.3, p. 11)
Limitations / Future Work: Author-acknowledged limitations: rapid obsolescence of AI-cybersecurity findings; data bias and limited generalizability of detection studies; reliance on simulation constrains ecological validity; underreported adversarial vulnerabilities; language/indexing bias (Sec. 2.7, p. 9); selection bias, human-interpretation subjectivity, heterogeneous metrics, publication bias, temporal limitation (Sec. 5.8, p. 20). Future work in phased horizons: short-term XAI and adversarial defense (1-3 yrs); medium-term federated learning with quantum-safe protocols (3-7 yrs); long-term neurosymbolic AI and quantum-enhanced multi-agent reinforcement learning (7+ yrs); gaps include benchmarking cognitive autonomy and human-agent trust calibration (Sec. 5.7, p. 20; Table 6, p. 19)
Relevance to My Thesis: This review supplies conceptual vocabulary directly transferable to an Agentic AI copilot for incident response: its design-pattern taxonomy (especially Human-in-the-Loop threat-triage assistants in SOCs and hybrid DRL+LLM human-agent architectures) mirrors the copilot orchestration model my thesis targets, and its autonomy-level taxonomy helps position a copilot between semi-autonomous assistance and full autonomy. Its evidence that agentic systems improve incident response efficiency, while noting that conceptual work dominates over empirical deployment, reinforces my thesis gap: the absence of measured MTTD/MTTR outcomes for agentic approaches. The governance discussion (human oversight, EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF) informs the human-in-the-loop accountability design of a production copilot. However, the paper is cybersecurity-centric (not SRE/AIOps) and offers no incident metrics I can reuse as baselines.
Relevance Score: Medium - adjacent: it reviews agentic/multi-agent architectures, human-in-the-loop patterns, and autonomous incident response in cybersecurity, but reports no MTTD/MTTR measurements and does not address IT-operations observability or AIOps directly.

Title: Analysing the role of LLMs in cybersecurity incident management
Authors: Gavin Jones; Dimitrios Kasimatis; Nikolaos Pitropakis; Richard Macfarlane; William J. Buchanan
Year & Venue: 2025; International Journal of Information Security (Springer), vol. 24, article 228; DOI 10.1007/s10207-025-01144-7
Core Problem Addressed: Organizations struggle to manage increasingly sophisticated cyber threats, and the traditional linear five-phase incident response model can cause delays and fail to adequately manage complex incidents; the paper investigates whether generative AI/LLMs can effectively enhance cybersecurity incident response processes (Sec. 1, p. 1; Sec. 2.1, p. 2)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: A purpose-built tool acting as an "incident response assistant or copilot": user-supplied incident details are wrapped in a fixed CLEAR-framework prompt and sent programmatically to OpenAI LLMs (gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4-0125-preview, gpt-4o, o1-preview) via API, which return actionable mitigation steps; three escalating context levels are used — zero-shot (no runbook), generalized NIST 800-61 runbook, and runbook plus prior-incident handling examples; single-LLM design (not multi-agent), with a client-server architecture (local Python client, OpenAI cloud API) and default model settings; human-in-the-loop with analyst approval is recommended for deployment (Sec. 4.1, pp. 4-5; Sec. 4.2.1, p. 5; Sec. 6.1.1, p. 11)
Methodology: Controlled experiment: 10 real-world-inspired incident scenarios (DDoS, cloud data exfiltration, insider misuse, ransomware with lateral movement, web application compromise) mapped across the NIST 800-61 lifecycle, run against 4 OpenAI models under 3 context conditions, each repeated 10 times — "producing 1,200 model invocations in total"; evaluation combined quantitative metrics (BERTScore consistency, spaCy-based conciseness and coherence) and qualitative LLM-as-a-judge scoring by GPT-4o (relevancy, clarity, domain-specific terminology, logical coherence, each 1-10) (Sec. 4.1, p. 4; Sec. 4.3, pp. 6-7)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not specified — no MTTD, MTTR, alert-fatigue, or resolution-time measurements are reported; results are qualitative fitness-for-phase findings: GPT-4o and GPT-3.5 "exhibit high clarity, consistency and coherence" suiting real-time containment, isolation, eradication and recovery, while GPT-o1 and GPT-4 better support preparation and post-incident analysis; the authors defer timing metrics, proposing future studies "employ quantitative metrics such as mean response time" (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 6, p. 10; Sec. 7, p. 12)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Single-agent LLM copilot study, not a multi-agent system; key finding is that "there is no single LLM that meets all the criteria required for every area", motivating model-to-phase specialization (e.g., GPT-4 most concise at 14.6 words/sentence in stage 2; GPT-3.5 most consistent BERTScore 0.4938 but lowest LLM-judged logical coherence 7.8; GPT-o1 highest relevancy ~9.1 and domain terminology 9.2); token context limits and hallucination risk constrain deployment; related multi-agent LLM incident-response work (Liu's AutoBnB tabletop framework) is reviewed as limited to controlled exercises; risk mitigation prescribes human-in-the-loop approval, dual control for irreversible steps, staged shadow/advisory rollout, audit logging, and least-privilege access (Sec. 3, p. 3; Sec. 5, pp. 8-10; Sec. 6, pp. 10-11; Appendix A, p. 12)
Limitations / Future Work: Limitations: reliance on a single LLM judge (GPT-4o) and one fixed rubric introduces bias; qualitative scores "may not fully capture operational correctness"; token context window constraints (GPT-3.5 has half GPT-4's window); default model settings only; OpenAI-only model set; ethical risks of workforce deskilling and false sense of security; Future work: evaluate other generative models including locally hosted alternatives, experiment with RAG and iterative query methods, use varied manual human inputs for realism, employ quantitative metrics such as mean response time, and assess response usability with tailored scenarios and runbooks (Sec. 6, pp. 10-11; Sec. 7, p. 12)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper directly tests an LLM "copilot" for incident response — the same operational role my thesis assigns to Agentic AI — and its three-level context design (zero-shot, runbook, runbook plus historical incidents) offers a reusable experimental blueprint for evaluating copilot guidance quality during response. Its finding that different models suit different lifecycle phases (fast/clear models for containment and recovery vs. reasoning models for preparation and post-incident analysis) informs agent-role assignment in a multi-agent MTTD/MTTR pipeline. Its evaluation stack (BERTScore, spaCy conciseness/coherence, LLM-as-a-judge) and its human-in-the-loop risk mitigation controls are transferable to my methodology. However, it addresses cybersecurity incidents rather than SRE/AIOps operations, is single-agent, and measures response quality rather than MTTD/MTTR, leaving the time-metric gap my thesis targets — a gap the authors themselves flag via "mean response time" as future work.
Relevance Score: Medium — an empirical LLM incident-response copilot evaluation closely adjacent to the thesis topic, but single-agent, cybersecurity-focused, and without any MTTD/MTTR or resolution-time measurement

Title: Graph-Augmented Multi-Agent Robust Root Cause Analysis in AIOps
Authors: Haodong Zou; Yichen Zhao; Xin Chen; Ling Wang; Jinghang Yu; Long Yuan
Year & Venue: 2026; Computers, Materials & Continua (CMC), Tech Science Press; vol. 88(1):40; DOI 10.32604/cmc.2026.077908; Published 08 May 2026
Core Problem Addressed: Root cause analysis (RCA) in complex microservice systems traditionally requires human engineers to manually correlate fragmented multi-modal observability signals (metrics, traces, logs), a labor-intensive and error-prone process; existing AIOps/LLM methods suffer from single-modal limits, simplistic temporal alignment that misses semantic relationships, LLM hallucinations, and "causal confusion" (mistaking symptoms for root causes) (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 1, pp. 2-3)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: A Graph-Augmented Multi-Agent Framework in two phases: (1) Anomaly Fusion Graph (AFG) construction — hybrid log-trace alignment fusing semantic similarity with spatio-temporal consistency, with an LLM as "semantic arbitrator" for ambiguous cases and an LLM Summarizer generating per-node health reports; (2) Multi-Agent Collaborative Reasoning simulating a human SRE team: Diagnoser Agent (Chain-of-Thought state evaluation, Root Cause/Propagator/Healthy), Navigator Agent (fault-gradient topology traversal via latency deviation, error propagation rate, traffic volatility), Verifier Agent (Adversarial Validation Protocol: consistency check, causal sufficiency, counterfactual reasoning), and Coordinator Agent (Shared Diagnostic Context, stack-based backtracking); agent backend is the OpenAI GPT-4 API (Sec. 4, pp. 5-13; Sec. 5.1, pp. 14-15)
Methodology: Prototype implementation (Python 3.9, Drain3, OpenTelemetry, GPT-4 API) with controlled experiments on five datasets: Train Ticket (73 faults, 132,000+ traces, 7.7 million log messages), Online Boutique (56 faults), MSDS/OpenStack (80+ fault instances), AIOps Challenge 2025 (400 fault instances), self-collected OpenTelemetry Demo (45 fault scenarios over 7 days); baselines DeepTraLog (GNN) and Direct LLM Diagnosis; Precision/Recall/F1 metrics; mean ± std over 5 runs, paired t-tests; thresholds via grid search on 80/20 train/validation splits; server with Intel Xeon Gold 6248R, 512 GB RAM, 4x NVIDIA A100 (Sec. 5.1, pp. 13-15)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: No quantitative MTTD/MTTR results reported. MTTR is cited qualitatively as motivation: the human-centric process is "labor-intensive and time-consuming, often leading to prolonged Mean Time To Repair (MTTR)" (Sec. 4.2, p. 10). Related time indicators: average end-to-end diagnosis latency of 21.4 s per fault (3.3 s AFG build + 18.1 s reasoning) and cost of approximately $0.15 per fault at GPT-4 Turbo pricing (Sec. 5.2.5, pp. 17-18)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Multi-agent framework achieves average F1-score 88.4% (±0.9), outperforming DeepTraLog (83.8%) by 4.6 percentage points and Direct LLM Diagnosis (71.4%) by 17.0 points, p < 0.01 (Table 2, Sec. 5.2.1, p. 15); log-trace alignment reaches 97.5% avg F1 vs. 68.9% temporal-window baseline (Table 3, p. 16); consensus-based verification lifts Precision from 79.5% (no verification) to 88.1% (Table 4, p. 17); ablation: removing Verifier drops Precision -8.5%, removing backtracking drops Recall -13.6%, random navigation degrades F1 to 75.3% (Table 5, p. 17); overhead: 3-5 agent calls per fault, avg 9.7K tokens, LLM arbitration triggered for 13.8%-20.3% of log-trace pairs (Sec. 5.2.5, pp. 17-18)
Limitations / Future Work: Failure rates 8.2%-11.3% per dataset; primary failure mode is ambiguous propagation chains (59% of failures) where simultaneous similar symptoms mislead the Diagnoser; insufficient log semantics (28%) with generic messages like "Error occurred"; in dense topologies (fan-out > 10) backtracking "degrades to near-exhaustive search"; in 12% of AIOps instances it exceeds 5 iterations, increasing latency by approximately 40%; LLM arbitration (94.2% accuracy) errs on domain-specific jargon and time windows < 10 ms; data unavailable due to privacy/ethical restrictions; no explicit future-work agenda stated (Sec. 5.2.6, Table 7, p. 18; Availability of Data, p. 19)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper is a strong architectural reference for an Agentic AI copilot in incident response: its four-role multi-agent design (Diagnoser, Navigator, Verifier, Coordinator) explicitly emulates SRE workflows and directly targets the diagnosis stage that drives MTTR, which the authors themselves cite as the motivating metric. The adversarial Verifier and backtracking mechanisms offer concrete, evaluated patterns for making LLM copilots trustworthy during incidents, addressing hallucination — a key risk for production copilots. Its runtime/cost analysis (21.4 s and ~$0.15 per fault) provides a rare operational feasibility datapoint for estimating time-to-diagnosis gains versus manual RCA. However, since it reports F1 rather than MTTD/MTTR, the thesis would need to map localization accuracy and diagnosis latency onto incident metrics.
Relevance Score: Medium — a multi-agent LLM AIOps framework highly aligned with agentic incident diagnosis, but it evaluates RCA accuracy (F1) and latency rather than directly measuring MTTD/MTTR.

Title: Empirical Study on Automation, AI Trust, and Framework Readiness in Cybersecurity Incident Response
Authors: Olufunsho I. Falowo; Jacques Bou Abdo
Year & Venue: 2026; Algorithms (MDPI journal), vol. 19, article 62; Received 2 December 2025, Published 11 January 2026
Core Problem Addressed: Legacy incident response frameworks (NIST, SANS) and current automation tools may be unready for AI-driven threats, and a research gap exists in understanding how practitioners navigate fragmented SOAR integration and under-deployed automation in critical phases like detection, triage, and containment, which diminishes its potential to reduce MTTD and MTTR (Sec. 1, p. 1; Sec. 2.6, p. 4)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: No system or architecture is proposed; the paper empirically quantifies practitioner perceptions of intelligent automation and agentic AI adoption in IR. Agentic AI was defined for respondents as "autonomous or semi-autonomous AI systems capable of perceiving their environment, reasoning through complex objectives, and taking independent actions" (e.g., dynamically updating firewall rules, isolating compromised nodes), distinct from linear scripted automation; findings are positioned as the empirical foundation for a future modular, AI-ready IR framework with AI-specific risk models, decision auditability, and human-in-the-loop mechanisms (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 4.1.2, p. 12; Sec. 6.4, p. 29; Table 5, p. 30)
Methodology: Structured, two-part quantitative survey (empirical study): 10 binary Yes/No items on automation/AI trust (RQ1) + 10 binary items on framework readiness (RQ2), plus psychometric validation items; 194 valid responses from U.S.-based cybersecurity professionals (target n=140 from population of 613,500 Computer and Information Systems Managers, 95% confidence, 4.97% margin of error, 10% response proportion); hosted on Qualtrics, distributed via LinkedIn, ISC2, ISACA networks, open first week of September 2025 to first week of October 2025; IRB approved (Univ. of Cincinnati, Protocol 2025-0022-UC); reliability via Cronbach's alpha/KR-20: 0.82 (Part 1) and approximately 0.78 (Part 2) (Sec. 3.1-3.4, pp. 5-9; Sec. 4, p. 10; Sec. 5.2, pp. 23-24)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Perception-based only, no measured time values: 92% of respondents affirmed that "automation has significantly reduced the mean time to detect and respond (MTTD/MTTR)" in their organizations vs. 8% No; 95% CI for n=194: [88.2%, 95.8%]; the paper also identifies an "efficiency-capability paradox": despite the 92% MTTD/MTTR result, 70% believe current automation tools cannot keep pace with evolving AI-driven attacks; contrasts with a prior SLR [4] where only 38.89% of literature acknowledged automation relevance (Table 3, p. 11; Sec. 4.1.3, p. 12; Sec. 5.1, p. 23; Sec. 5.4-5.5, pp. 25-26)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: 84% report already integrating agentic AI systems into IR processes (95% CI n=194: [78.8%, 89.2%]); but only 13% trust AI-driven decision-making without human intervention in high-stakes scenarios; 37% support autonomous triage/containment without analyst oversight; only 17% believe benefits outweigh false positive/negative risks; 20% say AI workflows make IR playbooks obsolete; 74% report retraining teams for AI tools; 79% advocate a new classification/taxonomy of automation tools by level of agentic AI; 96% support industry-wide revision of IR frameworks to include AI/agentic threat dimensions; 79% of organizations lack a separate AI threat modeling process (Table 3, p. 11; Table 4, pp. 16-17; Sec. 5.3, p. 25; Sec. 5.6, pp. 26-27)
Limitations / Future Work: Binary Yes/No format may reduce "complex practitioner perspectives into oversimplified dichotomies"; possible sampling bias (AI-engaged respondents overrepresented) and purposive/convenience sampling via professional networks, so the 4.97% margin of error should be interpreted with caution; U.S.-only sample limits global generalizability; self-reported perception data carry response bias; construct validity bias and framing effects acknowledged; future work: Likert scales, semi-structured interviews, case studies, longitudinal research, and a framework modernization study with a validation roadmap (external discussions, pilot studies, iterative adjustments) (Sec. 5.1, p. 23; Sec. 6, p. 27; Sec. 6.2-6.4, pp. 28-29)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper provides direct empirical practitioner evidence for the thesis premise: 92% of 194 U.S. cybersecurity professionals report that automation significantly reduced MTTD/MTTR, and 84% already integrate agentic AI into incident response, confirming the operational reality of the research topic. The pronounced trust gap (13% trust in fully autonomous decisions; 63% oppose unsupervised triage) strongly supports the thesis framing of Agentic AI as a copilot with human-in-the-loop oversight rather than a fully autonomous responder. Its survey instrument, psychometric validation (Cronbach's alpha), and sample size calculation offer a reusable methodological model if the thesis includes a practitioner survey. However, since MTTD/MTTR impact is perceptual (Yes/No) rather than measured in time units, the thesis should treat it as motivation and context, not as quantitative baseline evidence.
Relevance Score: High - the study empirically quantifies agentic AI adoption and perceived MTTD/MTTR reduction in incident response with 194 practitioners, directly matching the thesis topic, though impact is perception-based rather than measured in time units.

Title: Multi-Agent Coordination Strategies vs. Retrieval-Augmented Generation in LLMs: A Comparative Evaluation
Authors: Irina Radeva; Ivan Popchev; Lyubka Doukovska; Miroslava Dimitrova
Year & Venue: 2025; Electronics (MDPI), vol. 14, article 4883
Core Problem Addressed: Not an IT-operations paper: it targets the open question of whether multi-agent coordination added to already-configured RAG systems enhances or degrades performance versus calibrated single-agent RAG baselines, since prior multi-agent evaluations compare only against simple prompting baselines and use resource-intensive setups (iterative debates, 70B+ models); whether coordination overhead is justified for resource-constrained open-source deployments was unexamined (Sec. 1, pp. 1-2)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Comparative evaluation of four multi-agent coordination strategies — Collaborative (3 parallel peer agents with consensus aggregation, later improved with Two-Phase Consensus using a highest-confidence lead synthesizer), Sequential (Agent 1 -> Agent 2 -> Agent 3 progressive refinement), Competitive (3 parallel agents, highest-confidence winner selected), Hierarchical (2 specialists + 1 manager synthesizer) — implemented in the extended PaSSER framework (Python Flask/FastAPI API, React frontend, ChromaDB vector DB, LangChain RAG pipeline, Ollama/MLX local inference, blockchain result verification via Antelope); all agents in a configuration use the same base model (Mistral 7B, Llama 3.1 8B, or Granite 3.2 8B); two retrieval modes (independent vs. shared context, similarity threshold 0.95, k=5); no human-in-the-loop design is described (Sec. 3.1-3.2, pp. 5-9; Fig. 1, p. 6)
Methodology: Controlled experiment (comparative empirical evaluation): 100 question-answer pairs from the FAO Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook; 31 configurations in 4 groups (3 single-agent RAG baselines, 12 Original, 4 Granite-SCR, 12 Optimized) totaling 3100 evaluations (2800 multi-agent + 300 baseline); baselines tuned via a separate 369-question threshold evaluation (0.95 Mistral/Granite, 0.90 Llama); nine metrics aggregated into CPS (SAW-based MCDM) and T-CPS (alpha=0.1, beta=0.05); paired t-tests, Cohen's d, 95% CIs, sensitivity analysis over 25 parameter combinations; hardware: Intel Xeon CPU (Mistral, Granite) and Apple M1 (Llama) (Sec. 3.2-3.4, pp. 6-14; Sec. 4.1, p. 15)
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: Not applicable — the study evaluates factual question-answering quality (CPS/T-CPS) in an agriculture domain; no MTTD, MTTR, alert fatigue, or incident resolution metrics are reported (entire paper; Sec. 3.3, pp. 9-13)
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: All 28 multi-agent configurations degraded versus single-agent RAG baselines, from -4.39% (Mistral-Opt Hierarchical) to -35.31% (Granite Collaborative), all p < 0.01, effect sizes |d| = 0.28-6.09; Collaborative was worst across all models (-20.68% to -35.31%); shared context retrieval recovered 4.2-12.5 percentage points but coordination overhead remained the dominant degradation factor; Collaborative consumed 58.2% more tokens (mean 2656 vs. 1658-1717) via 3-4 inference calls per query vs. 1 for baseline; a "stable mediocrity" pattern showed consensus reduces variability while converging on lower-quality answers; conclusion: "single-agent RAG may be preferable for factual question-answering tasks in local deployment scenarios with computational constraints" (Sec. 4.2-4.8, pp. 15-23; Table 4, pp. 16-17; Table 5, p. 19; Abstract, p. 1)
Limitations / Future Work: Limitations: single domain (FAO agriculture QA), only 7-8B parameter models, homogeneous agent architectures (same base model per configuration), AI-generated role prompts (GitHub Copilot with Claude Sonnet), simple consensus without iterative refinement or explicit conflict resolution, heterogeneous hardware precluding cross-model timing comparison; findings should not be generalized to multi-step reasoning or larger scales; future work: role-specific prompting, advanced consensus (structured argumentation, learned aggregation, weighted voting), adaptive strategy selection, joint retrieval-coordination tuning, 70B+ models, heterogeneous agent teams (Sec. 5.3, pp. 26; Sec. 6, p. 27)
Relevance to My Thesis: This paper is a cautionary counterweight for the thesis's agentic incident-response copilot design: it empirically shows that naively adding multi-agent coordination to a working RAG pipeline can degrade output quality by 4-35% while multiplying token cost and latency (3-4 inference calls per query), which would directly inflate MTTR-relevant response times rather than reduce them. Its taxonomy of coordination strategies (collaborative, sequential, competitive, hierarchical) and the finding that selection-based strategies beat consensus-based synthesis inform which orchestration model an AIOps copilot should adopt. The CPS/T-CPS composite evaluation with a stability (consistency) term offers a transferable pattern for evaluating copilot answer quality and reliability in production incident scenarios. However, it contains no incident-management context or MTTD/MTTR measurements, so it supports architectural and evaluation-design decisions rather than the thesis's core metrics.
Relevance Score: Medium — it rigorously quantifies efficacy, overhead, and failure modes of multi-agent LLM coordination (a priority theme for copilot architecture choices) but addresses agricultural question-answering with no incident-response or MTTD/MTTR measurement.

Title: A Comprehensive Survey on LLM-Based Network Management and Operations
Authors: Jibum Hong; Nguyen Van Tu; James Won-Ki Hong
Year & Venue: 2025; International Journal of Network Management (IJNM), Wiley; vol. 35, no. 6, e70029; DOI 10.1002/nem.70029
Core Problem Addressed: Growing network scale, traffic demand, and heterogeneity (SDN/NFV, 5G/B5G, MEC) make traditional manual and rule-based network management inadequate: fixed policies, passive/reactive management, and limited scalability hinder performance and reliability; the paper surveys how LLMs can address these gaps versus ML/DL/RL and IBN approaches (Sec. 1, pp. 1-2; Sec. 2.1.1, pp. 3-4)
Proposed Solution / Agentic AI Role: Comprehensive survey of LLM-based approaches across five network management tasks: design, configuration, fault management, security, and orchestration (automation/optimization); reviews domain adaptation techniques (fine-tuning/LoRA, prompt engineering/CoT, RAG, feedback-based adaptation including RLHF, human-in-the-loop, self-refinement) (Sec. 2.2.2, pp. 7-8; Sec. 3, pp. 8-12); covers agentic/multi-agent case studies such as CommLLM (GPT-3.5 multiagent framework for 6G), multiagent GPT-4 collective-intelligence power saving, multi-agent LLM slicing management, MAPE-K closed-loop policy generation, and multiagent debate (MAD) (Sec. 4.1.2, p. 16; Sec. 4.5.1, pp. 35-36; Table 9, pp. 39-42); recommends LLMs "as auxiliary tools augmented with human verification" rather than replacing human network managers (Sec. 5.1.4, p. 44)
Methodology: Literature survey with case-by-case analysis: reviews and compares LLM-based network management studies against rule-based and ML/DL/RL methods, analyzing methods, contributions, limitations, and differences per study; compares itself with 7 existing LLM-based surveys (Table 1, p. 3); no systematic review protocol (e.g., search strings, inclusion criteria, or study count) is reported (Sec. 1, pp. 2-3; Sec. 4, pp. 13-42); Not specified: dataset and sample size for the survey itself
Impact on MTTD & MTTR Metrics: MTTD/MTTR are not measured; qualitative claim that LLM-based fault management strengthens resilience by "minimizing service downtime due to faults" across monitoring, analysis, detection/prediction, and recovery stages (Sec. 3.3, p. 11); reported metrics from surveyed studies are detection/diagnosis accuracies, not time-to-detect/recover: WirelessLLM 91% anomaly detection accuracy; MSADM 89% fault diagnosis accuracy; LogGPT F1 0.618 (BGL) and 0.694 (Spirit); Ciri up to 45% higher configuration error detection; Kwon et al. 48% Ansible script error correction accuracy (Sec. 4.3, pp. 23-27); intent-assurance study maintained 99.99% availability while improving intent drift detection and correction speed by three times (Sec. 4.5.1, p. 36); alert fatigue Not specified
General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Age: Multiagent GPT-4 system achieved "over 5% power savings" in wireless networks (Sec. 4.5.2, p. 38); CommLLM multiagent framework noted for unaddressed slow response time needing real-world verification (Sec. 4.1.2, p. 16); reported failure modes: hallucination propagating faulty configurations through closed-loop controllers, semantic inconsistency, unstable coordination among multiple agents, and limited runtime adaptability (Sec. 5.1.2, p. 43; Sec. 4.5.2, p. 38); overhead/cost: 13B-parameter model consumes about 26 GB memory, digital-twin verification adds tens to hundreds of milliseconds per request, and inference latency conflicts with sub-second control loops in carrier-grade networks (Sec. 5.1.1, p. 43; Sec. 5.1.2, p. 43); autonomy currently limited to auxiliary use with human verification (Sec. 5.1.4, p. 44)
Limitations / Future Work: Open challenges: real-time processing/performance (inference latency, memory, power), hallucination and output verification, domain-specific adaptation and legacy system (OSS, SDN/NFV) integration, reliability/explainability of LLM-generated rationales, and security/privacy (prompt injection, data leakage, inference attacks) (Sec. 5.1, pp. 42-44); future directions: lightweight/efficient LLMs (pruning, distillation, quantization, LoRA), modular MoE-style domain-specific LLMs, integration with existing rule-based/ML/DRL systems and human-in-the-loop frameworks, distributed edge-cloud inference and offloading, and enhanced reliability/security/privacy (adversarial training, XAI, federated learning, sandbox validation, accountability guidelines) (Sec. 5.2, pp. 44-46); the authors note the survey mostly covers studies evaluated in simulation with limited real-world validation (Sec. 4.3, p. 27; Sec. 4.5.2, p. 38)
Relevance to My Thesis: This survey maps the LLM-for-operations landscape adjacent to my thesis: its fault management taxonomy (monitoring, analysis, detection/prediction, recovery) mirrors the incident response pipeline where an Agentic AI copilot would act to reduce MTTD and MTTR. It catalogs concrete copilot-style systems (DIO Copilot, GeNet co-pilot, OCE-Helper incident management, HuntGPT) and multi-agent frameworks, plus the human-in-the-loop positioning that matches my copilot framing. Crucially, it confirms a gap my thesis can exploit: surveyed studies report accuracy/F1 rather than time-based incident metrics, so MTTD/MTTR measurement of agentic approaches is largely absent. Its challenge analysis (hallucination, latency, verification pipelines, digital-twin pretesting) provides design constraints and evaluation criteria for a trustworthy incident-response copilot.
Relevance Score: Medium - adjacent AIOps/network operations survey covering LLM-based fault management, copilots, and some multi-agent systems, but it does not measure MTTD/MTTR or incident time metrics with an agentic approach
